title: URL to pixels
text: 5 journeys: DNS (name → IP) → TCP (connection) → TLS (encrypt + verify) → HTTP (request) → render (HTML → pixels). See it: DevTools → Network → first request → Timing (DNS Lookup, Initial connection, SSL, Waiting, Content Download). Trap: DNS isn't done every visit — browser, OS and resolver cache it. First load is usually slowest.
html:
• 5 journeys: DNS (name → IP) → TCP (connection) → TLS (encrypt + verify) → HTTP (request) → render (HTML → pixels).
  • See it: DevTools → Network → first request → Timing (DNS Lookup, Initial connection, SSL, Waiting, Content Download).
  • Trap: DNS isn't done every visit — browser, OS and resolver cache it. First load is usually slowest.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Typing a URL and seeing a page takes five journeys: DNS (find the server), TCP (connect), TLS (make it private), HTTP (ask for the page), render (turn code into pixels).
  • The first four are network work, mostly waiting. The last one is browser work, mostly computing.
  • Every speed trick in web performance makes one of these five steps shorter, or skips it.

Interview answer

First the browser resolves the domain to an IP using DNS, checking caches before asking a resolver. Then it opens a TCP connection and, for HTTPS, does a TLS handshake to encrypt and verify the server. It sends an HTTP request and gets back HTML. Finally it parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, builds the render tree, and runs layout, paint and compositing to draw pixels. Subresources like CSS, JS and images trigger the same fetch cycle in parallel.

The analogy

Ordering food from a new restaurant. You look up its number (DNS), call and wait for someone to pick up (TCP), confirm it's really them and agree on a private line (TLS), place your order (HTTP), then the kitchen cooks and plates it (rendering). Most of the time is spent waiting, not cooking.

How it works

  • Steps 1–3 happen once per connection, not per file. That's why reusing connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2) matters so much.
  • While parsing the HTML, the browser finds <link>, <script> and <img> tags and fetches them too, often in parallel.
  • Each round trip costs real time. India to a US server is roughly 200 ms there and back, so 3 round trips = over half a second before the first byte.

Common traps

  • "DNS happens on every visit." Usually not. Browser, OS and resolver caches answer most lookups instantly. The first visit is the slowest.
  • "The page appears when the HTML arrives." No. CSS blocks rendering and synchronous scripts block parsing, so the page waits for them too.
  • Forgetting it repeats. Every CSS, JS, image and font file goes through fetch again (minus DNS/TCP/TLS if the connection is reused).

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → reload → click the first request → Timing tab. You'll see each phase: DNS Lookup, Initial connection, SSL, Waiting (server time), Content Download.

Quick quiz

Which of the five steps can a CDN shorten?

TCP, TLS and HTTP: the server is physically closer, so every round trip is shorter. It can also serve cached files without waiting for the origin.

Why is the first visit to a site slower than the second?

Nothing is cached yet: DNS answer, connection, and files (HTML/CSS/JS/images) all have to be fetched. On repeat visits the browser cache and connection reuse skip much of it.

What does "Waiting (TTFB)" in DevTools measure?

Time to First Byte: from sending the request until the first byte of the response arrives, which is mostly server processing plus one round trip.

title: DNS
text: Phonebook of the internet: domain → IP address. Resolver walks root → TLD (.com) → authoritative name servers. Answers carry a TTL ; cached until it expires. Try: nslookup google.com . Trap: after a server move some users hit the old IP until TTL expires → lower TTL before migrating.
html:
• Phonebook of the internet: domain → IP address.
  • Resolver walks root → TLD (.com) → authoritative name servers. Answers carry a TTL; cached until it expires.
  • Try: nslookup google.com. Trap: after a server move some users hit the old IP until TTL expires → lower TTL before migrating.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Computers talk using IP addresses (142.250.183.14), humans type names (google.com). DNS turns one into the other.
  • Your browser asks a resolver, which walks a chain of servers: root → TLD (.com) → the domain's own name server.
  • Every answer comes with a TTL (time to live). Everyone along the way caches it until it expires. That is why DNS is fast most of the time, and why changes take time to reach everyone.

Interview answer

DNS converts a domain name into an IP address. The browser first checks its own cache and the OS cache, then asks a recursive resolver. On a miss, the resolver asks a root server, then the TLD server like .com, then the domain's authoritative name server, and caches the answer for its TTL. For performance I keep third-party domains few and use dns-prefetch or preconnect for the ones I can't avoid.

The analogy

Think of your phone's contacts app. You tap "Mom", the phone dials +91 98xxx xxxxx. You never remember the number; the app does.

DNS is the contacts app of the internet, except nobody has the full list. So when your browser meets a name it hasn't seen, it has to ask around: first a general directory that knows who handles .com names, then the .com office that knows who handles google.com, then Google's own server that finally says the number.

How it actually works

When you type www.example.com and press Enter, your browser does not go to the internet straight away. It checks the cheapest places first:

  1. Browser cache. Chrome remembers recent answers for a short while.
  2. Operating system cache (and the hosts file on your laptop).
  3. The recursive resolver. Usually run by your ISP (Jio, Airtel) or a public one like 8.8.8.8 (Google) or 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare). This server does the legwork for you.

If the resolver doesn't have the answer cached, it walks the tree:

  • Root servers know who runs every top-level domain (.com, .in, .org). There are 13 named root server identities, each copied to hundreds of locations worldwide.
  • TLD servers know which name servers are in charge of each domain under them.
  • The authoritative name server is the one the domain owner controls (Cloudflare, Route 53, GoDaddy…). It holds the real records.

The resolver remembers every step. The next person asking for any .com name skips the root, and anyone asking for example.com within the TTL gets an instant answer.

The records you'll actually meet

Record Maps Example
A name → IPv4 address example.com → 93.184.215.14
AAAA name → IPv6 address example.com → 2606:2800:…
CNAME name → another name (alias) www.shop.com → shop.netlify.app
MX where email for the domain goes → mail.google.com
TXT free text, used for verification Google / SPF verification strings
NS which servers are authoritative → ns1.cloudflare.com

TTL: the reason "DNS propagation" exists

Each answer says how long it may be cached, for example TTL 3600 = one hour. If you move your site to a new server and update the A record, people whose resolver cached the old answer keep going to the old server until their copy expires. Nothing is "propagating"; old caches are simply timing out.

Why frontend engineers should care

A DNS lookup on a cold cache costs anything from ~20 ms to a few hundred ms, and it happens before a single byte of your page can download. Every new domain your page uses (fonts, analytics, ad scripts, an image CDN) can cost another lookup.

You can tell the browser to start early:

<!-- Look up the name early (cheap) -->
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
<!-- Look up + connect (TCP + TLS) early: use for the 1–3 domains you will definitely hit -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

See it yourself

  • Terminal: nslookup google.com or dig google.com (shows the TTL counting down if you run it twice).
  • Trace the full walk: dig +trace google.com.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network → click the first request → Timing tab → the DNS Lookup bar. Reload with cache disabled to see it grow.

Real-world story

On 4 October 2021, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp disappeared for about six hours. A maintenance command cut Facebook's data centers off, and its DNS servers, built to step back when they couldn't reach the data centers, withdrew themselves from the internet. With nobody able to answer "where is facebook.com?", the apps simply couldn't be found. (We made a reel about it: The day Facebook vanished.)

Common mistakes

  • Changing DNS with a long TTL. Lower the TTL (say to 300 s) a day before a migration, switch, then raise it again.
  • Putting a CNAME on the root domain (example.com itself). The standard doesn't allow it next to other records; use your provider's ALIAS/"CNAME flattening" instead.
  • Assuming DNS is free. Third-party scripts on five different domains = five lookups on a slow phone network.

Interview questions

Walk me through what DNS does when I type a URL.

Browser cache → OS cache/hosts file → recursive resolver. On a miss, the resolver asks a root server (which points to the TLD servers), then the TLD server (which points to the domain's authoritative servers), then the authoritative server, which returns the record with a TTL. Every layer caches the answer.

Recursive vs iterative queries?

Your device sends a recursive query: "give me the final answer". The resolver then makes iterative queries to root, TLD and authoritative servers, each of which only points to the next server.

Does DNS use UDP or TCP?

Mostly UDP on port 53, because it's one small question and one small answer. It falls back to TCP for large responses and zone transfers. Newer setups use DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or over TLS (DoT) to encrypt lookups.

A vs CNAME?

A points a name straight at an IP address. CNAME points a name at another name, which then has to be resolved too (an extra step, but you only update one place when the target's IP changes).

How can a frontend reduce DNS cost?

Use fewer third-party domains, self-host fonts and critical scripts, and add dns-prefetch/preconnect for the few domains you can't avoid.

title: TCP handshake
text: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = 1 round trip before any data (e.g. ~200 ms India ↔ US). Keep-alive reuses connections; later requests show 0 ms "Initial connection". Trap: TCP guarantees order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it (head-of-line blocking) → why HTTP/3 exists.
html:
• SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = 1 round trip before any data (e.g. ~200 ms India ↔ US).
  • Keep-alive reuses connections; later requests show 0 ms "Initial connection".
  • Trap: TCP guarantees order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it (head-of-line blocking) → why HTTP/3 exists.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Before any data moves, TCP does a three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK.
  • It costs one full round trip before the first request can even be sent.
  • TCP promises data arrives complete and in order, which is great, until one lost packet holds up everything behind it.

Interview answer

TCP is a reliable, ordered connection protocol. To open a connection the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK, which costs one round trip before any HTTP data. TCP then numbers every packet, retransmits lost ones and delivers them in order. That reliability causes head-of-line blocking, where one lost packet stalls everything behind it, which is a key reason HTTP/3 moved to QUIC over UDP.

The analogy

A phone call. You dial (SYN), they pick up and say "hello?" (SYN-ACK), you say "hi, it's me" (ACK). Only now does the real conversation start. And if a word gets garbled, you ask "sorry, say that again?" before moving on.

How it works

  • Sequence numbers let the receiver put packets back in order and spot gaps.
  • ACKs confirm what arrived. If an ACK doesn't come back, the sender retransmits.
  • Keep-alive reuses an open connection for the next request, so you don't pay the handshake again. In DevTools, reused connections show 0 ms "Initial connection".

Common traps

  • Head-of-line blocking. TCP must deliver in order, so if packet 3 is lost, packets 4–10 wait in the buffer even though they arrived fine.
  • HTTPS isn't one handshake. It's TCP first, then TLS on top: up to 2 round trips before the request (TLS 1.3 needs one).
  • "TCP is slow, UDP is fast." UDP just skips the guarantees. QUIC (HTTP/3) builds its own reliability on top of UDP without TCP's ordering problem.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → any request → Timing → Initial connection. Reload: the second time it's usually 0 because the connection was reused.

Quick quiz

How many round trips does a fresh HTTPS connection cost before the first request?

With TLS 1.3: 1 for TCP + 1 for TLS = 2. With TLS 1.2: 1 + 2 = 3. HTTP/3 (QUIC) combines them into 1, or 0 on resumed connections.

Why does keep-alive improve performance?

The connection stays open after a response, so the next request skips the TCP and TLS handshakes entirely.

What is TCP head-of-line blocking?

Because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, one lost packet blocks delivery of all later packets until it's retransmitted, even if they already arrived.

title: HTTPS & the padlock
text: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. 3 promises: encryption, integrity, authentication . Certificate chain: root CA (trusted by browser) → intermediate → site. TLS 1.3 handshake = 1 round trip (TLS 1.2 = 2). Trap: padlock = private connection, not a safe site. Phishing sites have valid certs.
html:
• HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. 3 promises: encryption, integrity, authentication.
  • Certificate chain: root CA (trusted by browser) → intermediate → site. TLS 1.3 handshake = 1 round trip (TLS 1.2 = 2).
  • Trap: padlock = private connection, not a safe site. Phishing sites have valid certs.
deep_html:
Key points

  • HTTPS = HTTP inside TLS. TLS gives three promises: encryption (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it), authentication (you're talking to the real site).
  • The site proves who it is with a certificate signed by a Certificate Authority your browser already trusts.
  • The padlock means the connection is private. It does not mean the site is safe or honest.

Interview answer

HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. During the TLS handshake the client and server agree on encryption keys using key exchange, and the server presents a certificate chain that the browser verifies up to a trusted root CA. After that, all traffic is encrypted and tamper-proof. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for the handshake. The padlock only guarantees a secure connection to that domain, not that the domain is trustworthy.

The analogy

Sending a letter in a locked box. Encryption: only the receiver has the key. Integrity: a broken seal shows tampering. Authentication: the box comes with an ID card stamped by a government office (the CA) you trust. The ID proves who they are, not that they're a nice person.

How it works

The certificate chain:

  • If any link fails (expired, wrong domain, untrusted issuer), the browser shows the full-page warning.
  • Free certificates (Let's Encrypt) made HTTPS the default; most browsers now flag plain HTTP as "Not secure".

Common traps

  • "Padlock = safe site." Phishing sites get valid certificates too. The padlock only proves the connection is encrypted to that domain.
  • Mixed content. An HTTPS page loading a script over http:// gets it blocked (scripts) or flagged (images).
  • "HTTPS is slow." With TLS 1.3, session resumption and HTTP/2 (which needs HTTPS in browsers), it's usually faster than plain HTTP.

See it yourself

Click the padlock / site-info icon → Connection is secure → Certificate is valid to see the chain. DevTools → Security tab shows the TLS version and cipher.

Quick quiz

What three things does TLS guarantee?

Confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tampering is detected), and authentication (the server proves its identity with a certificate).

How does the browser know a certificate is real?

It follows the chain of signatures from the site's certificate to an intermediate CA to a root CA that's in the browser/OS trust store, and checks the domain name and expiry.

Why is HTTP/2 usually only available over HTTPS?

Browsers only implement HTTP/2 over TLS (protocol negotiated during the TLS handshake via ALPN), so in practice HTTPS is required.

title: HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3
text: 1.1: one request per connection at a time → ~6 connections per site. 2: multiplexing + header compression on ONE TCP connection — but a lost packet stalls all streams. 3: QUIC over UDP, independent streams, survives Wi-Fi → mobile switches. Trap: HTTP/2 isn't always faster on lossy networks.
html:
• 1.1: one request per connection at a time → ~6 connections per site.
  • 2: multiplexing + header compression on ONE TCP connection — but a lost packet stalls all streams.
  • 3: QUIC over UDP, independent streams, survives Wi-Fi → mobile switches. Trap: HTTP/2 isn't always faster on lossy networks.
deep_html:
Key points

  • HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection, so browsers open about 6 connections per site.
  • HTTP/2: many requests at once on one connection (multiplexing) + compressed headers. But it still runs on TCP, so one lost packet stalls every stream.
  • HTTP/3: runs on QUIC over UDP. Streams are independent, handshakes are faster, and connections survive switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

Interview answer

HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers open around six parallel connections and requests queue behind each other. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over a single TCP connection and compresses headers, but a lost TCP packet blocks all streams. HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC on UDP, so each stream recovers loss independently, the handshake is combined with TLS, and connections can migrate between networks.

The analogy

A toll plaza. HTTP/1.1 = 6 booths, each car pays fully before the next moves. HTTP/2 = one huge booth processing many cars at once, but if one car breaks down, the whole lane stops. HTTP/3 = many independent lanes; a breakdown only blocks its own lane.

How it works

  • HTTP/1.1 tricks like domain sharding, sprites and bundling everything existed to work around the 6-connection limit. With HTTP/2 they're mostly unnecessary, sometimes harmful.
  • HTTP/2 server push was removed from Chrome; preload and 103 Early Hints replaced it.

Common traps

  • "HTTP/2 is always faster." On lossy mobile networks, one connection with TCP head-of-line blocking can lose to several HTTP/1.1 connections.
  • Confusing the two kinds of head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 fixed it at the HTTP level (requests no longer queue). HTTP/3 fixed it at the transport level (packet loss).
  • "UDP means unreliable." QUIC adds its own reliability and encryption on top of UDP.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → right-click the column header → enable Protocol. You'll see http/1.1, h2 and h3 side by side.

Quick quiz

What is multiplexing in HTTP/2?

Sending many requests and responses at the same time over one connection, split into interleaved frames tagged with stream IDs.

Why did HTTP/3 move away from TCP?

TCP's strict in-order delivery means one lost packet blocks all multiplexed streams, and TCP can't be changed easily because it lives in operating systems and middleboxes. QUIC on UDP fixes loss per stream and can evolve in user space.

Is bundling all JS into one big file still a good idea with HTTP/2?

Not necessarily. Many smaller files are cheap with multiplexing and cache better (one change doesn't invalidate everything). Very large numbers of tiny files still have overhead, so moderate code splitting wins.

title: CDNs
text: Copies of files on edge servers near users; hit = fast, miss = fetch once from origin then cache. Headers: x-cache , cf-cache-status , age . Trap: users see old assets after deploy → versioned (hashed) file names + purge.
html:
• Copies of files on edge servers near users; hit = fast, miss = fetch once from origin then cache.
  • Headers: x-cache, cf-cache-status, age.
  • Trap: users see old assets after deploy → versioned (hashed) file names + purge.
deep_html:
Key points

  • A CDN (Content Delivery Network) keeps copies of your files on servers close to users ("edges").
  • Cache hit: the edge already has the file, so it's fast. Cache miss: the edge fetches it once from your server (the "origin"), then serves everyone nearby.
  • The real win is distance: fewer milliseconds per round trip, and your origin doesn't melt under traffic.

Interview answer

A CDN is a network of edge servers around the world that cache copies of content close to users. A request goes to the nearest edge. On a hit, it's served directly with low latency; on a miss, the edge fetches from the origin, caches it based on the Cache-Control headers, and serves it. This reduces latency and offloads the origin. The main challenge is invalidation, which is usually solved with content-hashed filenames and long cache lifetimes, plus purges for HTML.

The analogy

A pizza chain. Instead of one kitchen in Mumbai delivering to all of India, there's an outlet in every city. Your order goes to the nearest outlet. If it doesn't have the topping, it gets it from the central warehouse once, then keeps it for the next customer.

How it works

# Static assets with a content hash in the name: cache "forever"
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable      → app.3f9a1c.js

# HTML: always check for a newer version
Cache-Control: no-cache                                   → index.html
  • CDNs also terminate TLS close to the user, so the handshakes are shorter too.
  • Response headers like x-cache: HIT, cf-cache-status: HIT and age: 1200 tell you whether you got a cached copy.

Common traps

  • "Users see the old version after deploy." Classic cache-invalidation bug. Fix: hashed filenames (app.3f9a1c.js) for assets, no-cache for HTML, and purge on deploy.
  • Caching personalized pages. If a response depends on cookies or login, a shared CDN cache can show one user's page to another. Use Cache-Control: private or vary correctly.
  • Single point of failure. If the CDN breaks, every site on it breaks (see the Fastly outage in our reels).

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → click a JS or image file → Headers → look for x-cache, cf-cache-status or age. Reload a few times and watch MISS turn into HIT.

Quick quiz

What's the difference between a cache hit and a miss at the edge?

Hit: the edge already has a fresh copy and responds immediately. Miss: it has to fetch from the origin first (slower), then caches the result for later requests.

How do you deploy new JS without users getting stale files from the CDN?

Put a content hash in the filename so every change is a new URL, cache those for a year with immutable, and keep HTML short-lived or no-cache so it always points to the latest hashed files.

Can a CDN help dynamic, non-cacheable pages?

Yes: shorter TLS/TCP handshakes to a nearby edge, optimized connections from edge to origin, compression, and edge compute. But the biggest wins are for cacheable static content.

title: DOM & CSSOM
text: HTML → DOM tree; CSS → CSSOM tree. CSS blocks rendering; classic <script> blocks parsing. View Source = what arrived; Elements = live DOM. Trap: DOM ≠ HTML (browser fixes markup, JS mutates it).
html:
• HTML → DOM tree; CSS → CSSOM tree. CSS blocks rendering; classic <script> blocks parsing.
  • View Source = what arrived; Elements = live DOM.
  • Trap: DOM ≠ HTML (browser fixes markup, JS mutates it).
deep_html:
Key points

  • The browser turns HTML into the DOM (a tree of objects) and CSS into the CSSOM (a tree of style rules).
  • CSS blocks rendering: nothing is painted until the CSS is loaded, otherwise you'd see a flash of unstyled page.
  • A normal <script> blocks parsing: the parser stops, downloads and runs it, then continues. defer and async fix that.

Interview answer

The browser parses HTML bytes into tokens and builds the DOM tree, and parses CSS into the CSSOM. CSS is render-blocking because the browser won't paint until it knows the styles. Classic synchronous scripts are parser-blocking because they might modify the DOM, so the parser pauses until they download and execute. Using defer or async, and putting critical CSS early, keeps the critical rendering path short.

The analogy

Building furniture from a manual. The HTML is the parts list: what pieces exist and how they fit (the DOM). The CSS is the paint and finish instructions (the CSSOM). You won't show the furniture to anyone until you know what colour it is. And if a step says "stop and read this other booklet first" (a script), you stop building until you've read it.

How it works

<!-- Blocks parsing until downloaded AND run -->
<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- Downloads in parallel, runs after parsing, in order: best default -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

<!-- Downloads in parallel, runs as soon as it arrives (order not guaranteed): good for analytics -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>
  • The parser streams: it builds the DOM as bytes arrive, it doesn't wait for the whole file.
  • A preload scanner looks ahead for <link>, <script> and <img> to start downloads early, even while parsing is blocked.

Common traps

  • "The DOM is the HTML." No. The browser fixes broken markup (adds missing <tbody>, closes tags), and JavaScript changes the DOM afterwards. View Source shows what arrived; the Elements panel shows the live DOM.
  • async vs defer. defer keeps order and waits for parsing to finish; async runs whenever it's ready, in any order.
  • Scripts in <head> without defer delay the whole page from showing up.

See it yourself

Compare View Page Source (raw HTML) with DevTools → Elements (live DOM) on any React site. The source is nearly empty; the DOM is full.

Quick quiz

Why is CSS render-blocking?

Painting without styles would show unstyled content and then reflow everything when CSS arrives (FOUC). So the browser waits for the CSSOM before the first paint.

When would you use async instead of defer?

For independent scripts that don't depend on the DOM or other scripts, such as analytics or ads, where order doesn't matter and you want them to run as early as possible.

Why doesn't the DOM always match the HTML source?

The parser repairs invalid markup, and JavaScript adds, removes and changes nodes after load.

title: Layout → Paint → Composite
text: Render tree (visible nodes) → Layout (size/position) → Paint (pixels) → Composite (GPU stacks layers). Performance panel: purple = layout, green = paint. Q: display:none removes from render tree (no space); visibility:hidden keeps the space.
html:
• Render tree (visible nodes) → Layout (size/position) → Paint (pixels) → Composite (GPU stacks layers).
  • Performance panel: purple = layout, green = paint.
  • Q: display:none removes from render tree (no space); visibility:hidden keeps the space.
deep_html:
Key points

  • After DOM + CSSOM, the browser runs a pipeline: render tree → layout → paint → composite.
  • Layout works out where and how big every box is. Paint fills in pixels (text, colours, shadows). Composite stacks painted layers on the GPU.
  • display: none removes an element from the render tree; visibility: hidden keeps its space.

Interview answer

The browser combines the DOM and CSSOM into a render tree of visible elements with their computed styles. Layout calculates the exact size and position of each box. Paint records drawing commands and rasterises them into layers, and compositing combines those layers on the GPU into the final frame. Changes later in the pipeline are cheaper: a transform only needs compositing, while a width change triggers layout, paint and composite again.

The analogy

Making a magazine page. Render tree: decide which articles make it in. Layout: draw the grid and box sizes on the page. Paint: print the text, photos and colours into each box. Composite: stack transparent sheets (layers) on top of each other to get the final page.

How it works

  • Layout depends on the parent: a box's width usually comes from its container, its height from its children, so changes ripple.
  • Some elements get their own layer (videos, transform/opacity animations, will-change), so they can move without repainting the rest.

Common traps

  • display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0. None: not in the render tree, no space. Hidden: takes space, not visible, not clickable. Opacity 0: takes space, invisible, still clickable.
  • "Paint means drawing to the screen." The screen update is the composite step; paint produces layer bitmaps.
  • Too many layers. Each one costs GPU memory; promoting everything makes things slower, not faster.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record a page load. Purple blocks are Layout (and style), green blocks are Paint. DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Layers shows each composited layer.

Quick quiz

What's in the render tree, and what isn't?

Visible nodes with computed styles. Not included: <head>, <script>, display: none elements and their children. visibility: hidden elements are included (they take space).

Order the stages: paint, layout, composite, style.

Style → Layout → Paint → Composite.

Why is animating transform cheaper than animating left?

left changes geometry, so every frame needs layout + paint + composite. transform is applied at composite time on an existing layer, so it skips layout and paint.

title: Reflow vs repaint
text: Geometry (width/height/top) → layout + paint + composite. Color → paint + composite. transform/opacity → composite only. Reflow spreads to siblings/parents. DevTools → Rendering → Paint flashing. Trap: reading offsetHeight right after a style write forces synchronous layout.
html:
• Geometry (width/height/top) → layout + paint + composite. Color → paint + composite. transform/opacity → composite only.
  • Reflow spreads to siblings/parents. DevTools → Rendering → Paint flashing.
  • Trap: reading offsetHeight right after a style write forces synchronous layout.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Reflow (layout): something's size or position changed, so the browser recalculates geometry, then repaints and composites. Expensive.
  • Repaint: only looks changed (colour, background, shadow), so it repaints and composites. Cheaper.
  • Composite-only: transform and opacity. Cheapest: no layout, no paint.

Interview answer

Changing geometry properties like width, height, top or font-size triggers layout, then paint and composite, and layout can cascade to parents, siblings and children. Changing visual-only properties like color or background triggers paint and composite. Changing transform or opacity on a layer only triggers compositing, which runs on the GPU. So for animations and frequent updates I stick to transform and opacity.

The analogy

Rearranging a classroom. Reflow: one desk gets bigger, so every desk in the row shifts and you re-measure the room. Repaint: you just change one desk's colour; nothing moves. Composite: you slide a transparent sheet with a drawing over the desks; the desks themselves are untouched.

How it works

// Expensive: layout every frame
box.style.left = x + 'px';

// Cheap: composite only
box.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;
  • One reflow can spread: changing a child's height can resize its parent and push its siblings.
  • Reading layout values (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect()) right after changing styles forces the browser to do layout immediately (next episode: layout thrashing).

Common traps

  • "Repaint is free." It's cheaper than layout, but painting large areas (big blurred shadows, full-page backgrounds) is still slow.
  • Forced synchronous layout. Write a style, then read a size, in the same frame = a reflow right now.
  • visibility vs display toggles. display changes trigger layout; visibility only repaints.

See it yourself

DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Rendering → tick Paint flashing. Green flashes show every area being repainted as you scroll and hover.

Quick quiz

Does changing color trigger a reflow?

No. Color doesn't affect geometry, so only paint and composite run.

Which two properties can be animated without layout or paint?

transform and opacity, when the element is on its own compositor layer.

Why is reflow considered expensive?

Geometry depends on other elements, so a change can force recalculation of parents, siblings and children, and then everything affected must be repainted.

title: Layout thrashing
text: Read/write/read/write in a loop → a layout per read. Fix: batch all reads, then all writes; schedule writes in requestAnimationFrame . Shows as "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck" in Performance. Q: layout-forcing reads: offsetHeight/Top, clientWidth, scrollTop, getBoundingClientRect().
html:
• Read/write/read/write in a loop → a layout per read. Fix: batch all reads, then all writes; schedule writes in requestAnimationFrame.
  • Shows as "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck" in Performance.
  • Q: layout-forcing reads: offsetHeight/Top, clientWidth, scrollTop, getBoundingClientRect().
deep_html:
Key points

  • Layout thrashing = writing styles and reading layout values back and forth in a loop. Every read forces a fresh layout.
  • 100 items × (write + read) = 100 layouts in one frame instead of 1.
  • Fix: read everything first, then write everything, ideally inside requestAnimationFrame.

Interview answer

The browser normally batches style changes and runs layout once per frame. But if you read a layout property like offsetHeight after writing a style, it has to run layout synchronously to give you a correct value. Doing that write-read pattern in a loop forces layout on every iteration, which is layout thrashing. The fix is to batch all reads first and then all writes, or schedule writes with requestAnimationFrame.

The analogy

Asking a tailor to measure you after every single stitch. "Add a button. How long is the sleeve now? Add another. How long now?" The tailor re-measures the whole shirt every time. Instead: take all measurements first, then do all the stitching.

How it works

// Bad: Thrashing: each read forces layout because the previous write made it dirty
for (const card of cards) {
  card.style.height = card.offsetWidth + 'px';   // read → write → read → write…
}

// Good: Batched: one layout for all reads, then writes are applied together
const widths = cards.map(c => c.offsetWidth);       // all reads
requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  cards.forEach((c, i) => c.style.height = widths[i] + 'px');   // all writes
});

Properties that force layout when read: offsetTop/Left/Width/Height, clientWidth/Height, scrollTop, scrollHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), getComputedStyle() (for layout values).

Common traps

  • "Reading is harmless." Reading is only free if nothing changed since the last layout.
  • Hidden in libraries. jQuery's .height(), measuring scroll position in a scroll handler, or a React effect that measures then sets state can all thrash.
  • Use observers instead of polling. ResizeObserver and IntersectionObserver give you sizes without forcing layout in your own code.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record. Thrashing shows as many tiny purple Layout blocks with a red corner and the warning "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck."

Quick quiz

Why does reading offsetHeight after setting a style cause layout?

The style change made layout invalid. To return an accurate number, the browser must recalculate layout immediately instead of waiting for the next frame.

How do you fix layout thrashing in a loop?

Do all reads first and store them, then do all writes (optionally in requestAnimationFrame), so layout runs once.

Name three properties that force layout when read.

offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), scrollTop (also clientWidth, offsetTop, scrollHeight).

title: Smooth animation
text: Animate transform / opacity (compositor, GPU layer) not left/top/width (layout every frame). will-change: transform hints a layer — each layer costs GPU memory, don't overuse. Check: Rendering → Frame Rendering Stats.
html:
• Animate transform/opacity (compositor, GPU layer) not left/top/width (layout every frame).
  • will-change: transform hints a layer — each layer costs GPU memory, don't overuse.
  • Check: Rendering → Frame Rendering Stats.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Smooth = 60 frames a second, about 16.7 ms per frame, including your JS, style, layout and paint.
  • Animate transform and opacity. They run on the compositor (GPU) and skip layout and paint.
  • will-change: transform promotes an element to its own layer ahead of time. Use it sparingly: every layer costs GPU memory.

Interview answer

For smooth 60 fps animation each frame has about 16 ms, so I avoid animating properties that cause layout or paint, like width, top or box-shadow. I animate transform and opacity, which can be handled by the compositor thread on the GPU, often even when the main thread is busy. I use CSS transitions or the Web Animations API, or requestAnimationFrame for JS-driven motion, and will-change only on elements that are about to animate.

The analogy

A flipbook. Each page must be drawn in time or the motion stutters. Animating left is like redrawing the whole page for every flip. Animating transform is like sliding a cut-out sticker across the same page: much faster.

How it works

.card { transition: transform 200ms ease, opacity 200ms ease; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02); }

/* Only for elements about to animate, remove when done */
.drawer.opening { will-change: transform; }
  • CSS transitions and animations on transform/opacity can keep running smoothly even if JavaScript blocks the main thread for a moment.
  • For JS-driven motion, use requestAnimationFrame and base movement on time, not on frame count.

Common traps

  • will-change on everything. Creates many layers, eats GPU memory, and can make things slower, especially on phones.
  • "translateZ(0) hack." It forces a layer like will-change, with the same costs. Know why it works before using it.
  • 120 Hz screens. The budget is about 8.3 ms per frame, so heavy JS hurts even more on modern phones.

See it yourself

DevTools → Rendering → tick Frame Rendering Stats (live FPS meter) and Layer borders. Compare animating left vs transform on the same element.

Quick quiz

Why is transform animation smoother than top/left?

It doesn't change layout, so the browser can skip layout and paint and just move an existing layer on the compositor, often on the GPU.

What does will-change do, and what's the risk?

It hints the browser to create a compositor layer in advance. Overusing it creates too many layers and wastes memory.

How many milliseconds per frame at 60 fps?

About 16.7 ms (1000 / 60), and the browser needs part of that for its own work, so aim for about 10 ms of your code.

title: One-chef kitchen
text: JS runs on one main thread that also does style, layout, paint. A 3 s loop freezes everything. Waiting (timers, fetch, events) happens in browser Web APIs; results come back through queues. Trap: setTimeout(fn, 0) = "as soon as possible", not "now".
html:
• JS runs on one main thread that also does style, layout, paint. A 3 s loop freezes everything.
  • Waiting (timers, fetch, events) happens in browser Web APIs; results come back through queues.
  • Trap: setTimeout(fn, 0) = "as soon as possible", not "now".
deep_html:
Key points

  • JavaScript in the browser runs on one main thread: one "chef" who also handles clicks, scrolling, style, layout and paint.
  • Waiting (timers, network, events) happens outside the chef, in the browser's Web APIs. Computing happens on the chef.
  • So a fetch() never freezes the page, but a long loop does. Anything over ~50 ms on the main thread is a long task, and users feel it.

Interview answer

JavaScript runs on a single main thread that also handles input, style, layout and paint. Waiting work like timers, network and events is handled by the browser's Web APIs, and their callbacks are queued and run when the main thread is free. That's why fetch doesn't freeze the page but a long loop does. To keep the UI responsive I break heavy work into chunks and yield, or move it to a Web Worker.

The analogy

A restaurant with exactly one cook. The cook makes your food, but also takes orders, plates dishes and wipes the counter. If one order takes the cook 3 minutes of chopping, every other table waits, even the person who just wants water.

The cook does have helpers: a timer on the oven, a delivery boy who fetches ingredients. They work on their own and leave a note on the counter when done. The cook reads the notes only when the hands are free.

How it actually works

The main thread runs one piece of work at a time. Here's the loop it repeats forever:

Meanwhile the Web APIs (timers, network, input) work on their own and drop finished jobs into the task queue.

  • Call stack: the function the chef is running right now, and the functions that called it.
  • Web APIs: the helpers. setTimeout, fetch, DOM events and so on are handled by the browser, not by your JavaScript.
  • Task queue: finished helper jobs waiting for the chef (a timer fired, a click happened, a response arrived).
  • Rendering: the browser tries to draw ~60 times a second (every ~16.7 ms), but only between tasks. If your task runs 3 seconds, no frames are drawn for 3 seconds. That's the "frozen" page.

Blocking vs not blocking

// Freezes the page for 3 seconds: the chef never gets a break.
const end = Date.now() + 3000;
while (Date.now() < end) {}

// Doesn't freeze anything: the waiting happens in the browser, not on the chef.
fetch('/api/orders').then(r => r.json()).then(render);
setTimeout(() => console.log('3 seconds later'), 3000);

How to do heavy work without freezing

1. Break it into chunks and give the chef a break between them:

async function processAll(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    heavyWork(items[i]);
    if (i % 200 === 0) {
      // Let clicks, scroll and paint happen, then continue.
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
    }
  }
}

2. Hire a second chef with a Web Worker, which runs on a separate thread (it can't touch the DOM, but it can crunch numbers):

// main.js
const worker = new Worker('worker.js');
worker.postMessage(bigArray);
worker.onmessage = e => showResult(e.data);

// worker.js
onmessage = e => postMessage(expensiveCalculation(e.data));

See it yourself

  • Open any site, paste the 3-second while loop in the Console, then try to scroll or click. Nothing responds until it ends.
  • DevTools → Performance → record while it runs. You'll see one long grey/yellow block with a red triangle: a long task.

Real-world connection

Google's INP (Interaction to Next Paint) metric, one of the Core Web Vitals, measures exactly this: how long after a tap the page actually paints a response. Busy main threads are the #1 cause of bad INP.

Common mistakes

  • "async makes it run in the background." It doesn't. An async function still runs on the main thread; only the waiting (await fetch) is offloaded.
  • Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs now. It means "add a task as soon as possible". It still waits for the current task (and all microtasks) to finish.
  • Parsing a huge JSON or sorting 1 lakh rows in a click handler. Chunk it, move it to a worker, or do it on the server.

Interview questions

Is JavaScript single-threaded? Then how does fetch not block?

Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but the browser is multi-threaded. fetch hands the request to the browser's network layer; when the response arrives, a callback is queued and runs when the main thread is free.

What's the output order? 
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
console.log('D');

A, D, C, B. Synchronous code first (A, D). Then all microtasks (the promise: C). Then the next task (the timer: B).

What is a long task and why does it matter?

Any task that keeps the main thread busy for more than 50 ms. During it the page can't respond to input or paint, so clicks feel laggy. It directly hurts INP.

How would you keep the UI responsive while processing a large dataset?

Split the work into chunks and yield between them (setTimeout, or scheduler.yield() where supported), move pure computation to a Web Worker, or paginate/virtualise so you don't process everything at once.

title: Call stack & task queue
text: log A; setTimeout(log B, 0); log C → A, C, B. Stack runs sync code; Web APIs hold timers; callbacks wait in the task queue; event loop moves a task when the stack is empty. Q: no true 0 ms — deeply nested timers clamp to ≥ 4 ms.
html:
• log A; setTimeout(log B, 0); log C → A, C, B.
  • Stack runs sync code; Web APIs hold timers; callbacks wait in the task queue; event loop moves a task when the stack is empty.
  • Q: no true 0 ms — deeply nested timers clamp to ≥ 4 ms.
deep_html:
Key points

  • The call stack is where JavaScript runs code right now, one function at a time.
  • Timers, clicks and network replies don't run immediately. They wait in the task queue.
  • The event loop moves the next task onto the stack only when the stack is empty. That's why setTimeout(fn, 0) still runs after your normal code.

Interview answer

JavaScript executes synchronous code on the call stack. Async callbacks like timers and events are handled by the browser and, when ready, placed in the task queue. The event loop checks whether the call stack is empty, and only then pushes the next task onto it. So setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't mean "now", it means "after the current code finishes".

The analogy

A chef with one to-do list. The stack is the dish in the chef's hands. The queue is the line of order slips on the counter. The chef never drops a half-made dish to read a new slip. Finish this one, then take the next slip.

How it works

console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
console.log('C');
// Output: A, C, B

A runs, the timer is handed to the browser, C runs. The stack is now empty, so the loop picks up the timer's callback: B.

Common traps

  • "0 ms means instant." It means "queue it as soon as possible", and it still waits for the stack to empty. Deeply nested timers are even clamped to at least 4 ms.
  • A slow function delays every timer. If the stack is busy for 2 seconds, a timer set for 100 ms fires after about 2 seconds.
  • Stack overflow is a different problem. Infinite recursion fills the stack ("Maximum call stack size exceeded"). It has nothing to do with the queue.

See it yourself

DevTools → Sources → add a breakpoint inside a function → the Call Stack panel on the right shows every function waiting to return.

Quick quiz

What's the output? 
setTimeout(() => console.log(1), 0);
for (let i = 0; i < 1e9; i++) {}
console.log(2);

2, then 1. The loop blocks the stack, so the timer's callback waits in the queue until the loop and console.log(2) are done.

Who decides when a queued callback runs?

The event loop. It runs one when the call stack is empty.

Where does the timer actually count down?

In the browser's Web APIs, not in JavaScript. JavaScript just gets a callback in the queue when the time is up.

title: Microtasks vs tasks
text: Tasks: timers, events. Microtasks: promise callbacks, queueMicrotask . After each task the loop drains ALL microtasks (incl. new ones), then may render, then next task. 1,timeout 2,promise 3,4 → 1 4 3 2. Trap: microtask starvation freezes the page.
html:
• Tasks: timers, events. Microtasks: promise callbacks, queueMicrotask.
  • After each task the loop drains ALL microtasks (incl. new ones), then may render, then next task. 1,timeout 2,promise 3,4 → 1 4 3 2.
  • Trap: microtask starvation freezes the page.
deep_html:
Key points

  • There are two queues. Tasks (macrotasks): setTimeout, setInterval, clicks, network events. Microtasks: promise .then/await continuations, queueMicrotask.
  • After every task, the browser runs all microtasks, including new ones added along the way, before it renders or takes the next task.
  • So promises always beat timers.

Interview answer

The event loop takes one task from the task queue and runs it. As soon as the call stack is empty, it drains the entire microtask queue, which holds promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks, including any microtasks queued during that drain. Only then can it render and move to the next task. That's why a resolved promise's then runs before a setTimeout of 0, and why an endless chain of microtasks can freeze the page.

The analogy

A doctor's clinic. Tasks are patients in the waiting room, seen one at a time. Microtasks are "one quick follow-up question" from the patient who's already in the room. The doctor answers all follow-ups before calling the next patient, even follow-ups to follow-ups.

How it works

console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);          // task
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); // microtask
console.log(4);
// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2

1 and 4 are synchronous. Then the microtask (3) runs, then the next task: the timer (2).

Common traps

  • await = microtask. The code after an await continues as a microtask, not right away.
  • Microtask starvation. A promise callback that keeps queueing another microtask never lets the browser render or handle clicks. The page freezes.
  • Order puzzle classic: sync code → microtasks → one task → microtasks → render → next task.

See it yourself

Paste the code above in the Console. Then try this to watch a timer get starved:

setTimeout(() => console.log('timer'), 0);
let n = 0;
function loop() { if (n++ < 1e6) queueMicrotask(loop); else console.log('done'); }
loop();   // 'done' prints before 'timer'

Quick quiz

What's the output? 
setTimeout(() => console.log('A'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log('B');
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
});
console.log('D');

D, B, C, A. The new microtask C is queued during the drain, so it runs before the timer.

Is the callback of an async function after `await` a task or a microtask?

A microtask: the continuation after await is scheduled like a promise .then.

Can microtasks block rendering?

Yes. Rendering only happens after the microtask queue is empty, so an endless microtask loop blocks paint and input.

title: 16 ms frame budget
text: 60 Hz ≈ 16.7 ms per frame (120 Hz ≈ 8.3 ms). Keep your JS ≲ 10 ms. requestAnimationFrame runs right before paint, once per frame, pauses in background tabs. Use its timestamp (time-based motion). setInterval drifts against frames.
html:
• 60 Hz ≈ 16.7 ms per frame (120 Hz ≈ 8.3 ms). Keep your JS ≲ 10 ms.
  • requestAnimationFrame runs right before paint, once per frame, pauses in background tabs. Use its timestamp (time-based motion).
  • setInterval drifts against frames.
deep_html:
Key points

  • On a 60 Hz screen the browser draws a frame every ~16.7 ms. On 120 Hz screens it's ~8.3 ms.
  • Your JS + style + layout + paint must fit inside that budget, or frames get dropped (jank). Aim for about 10 ms of your own work.
  • Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates: it runs once per frame, right before paint, and pauses in background tabs.

Interview answer

At 60 Hz each frame has about 16.7 ms, and the browser needs part of that for style, layout, paint and compositing, so my JavaScript should take roughly 10 ms or less per frame. For visual updates I use requestAnimationFrame, which runs right before the next paint and syncs with the display's refresh rate, and I compute motion from the timestamp it provides rather than assuming a fixed frame rate. setInterval isn't synced to frames, so it can drift and update twice or not at all in a frame.

The analogy

A train that leaves the platform every 16.7 ms, whether you're on it or not. If your work isn't done when it leaves, your update waits for the next train, and the user sees a stutter.

How it works

// Good: Smooth, time-based movement: same speed on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens
let start;
function step(now) {
  start ??= now;
  const x = Math.min((now - start) * 0.2, 300);   // 0.2 px per ms
  box.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;
  if (x < 300) requestAnimationFrame(step);
}
requestAnimationFrame(step);

Common traps

  • Frame-count based motion. x += 2 per frame moves twice as fast on a 120 Hz phone. Use the timestamp.
  • setInterval(fn, 16) for animation. Not aligned with paint: some frames get two updates, some get none.
  • Heavy work inside rAF. rAF doesn't make slow code fast; it only schedules it at the right moment.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record while scrolling or animating. The Frames row shows each frame; long red bars are dropped frames.

Quick quiz

What's the frame budget at 60 fps and 120 fps?

About 16.7 ms and 8.3 ms.

When does a requestAnimationFrame callback run?

Once per frame, just before the browser does style, layout and paint for that frame. It's paused in hidden tabs.

Why use the rAF timestamp instead of counting frames?

Refresh rates differ and frames can be dropped, so movement based on elapsed time stays the same speed on every device.

title: Long tasks
text: 50 ms = long task; blocks input. 100 ms feels instant (50 task + 50 input/paint). Fix: chunk work and yield ( await scheduler.yield() or setTimeout ). Metric: INP (Interaction to Next Paint), Core Web Vital since 2024 (replaced FID).
html:
• 50 ms = long task; blocks input. 100 ms feels instant (50 task + 50 input/paint).

  • Fix: chunk work and yield (await scheduler.yield() or setTimeout).
  • Metric: INP (Interaction to Next Paint), Core Web Vital since 2024 (replaced FID).
deep_html:
Key points

  • A long task is anything that keeps the main thread busy for more than 50 ms.
  • During a long task the page can't respond to taps or draw, so clicks feel laggy.
  • It's measured by INP (Interaction to Next Paint), a Core Web Vital since 2024 (it replaced FID). Fix: break the work up and yield.

Interview answer

A long task is any main-thread task over 50 ms. While it runs, input events and rendering wait, so the UI feels unresponsive, which shows up as poor INP. The 50 ms limit comes from aiming for a response within about 100 ms, leaving time for the browser to handle the input and paint. To fix it, I split the work into smaller chunks and yield back to the browser between them, move heavy computation to a Web Worker, or avoid doing the work at all with pagination or virtualisation.

The analogy

A single checkout counter. One customer with 300 items (a long task) holds up everyone behind them, even the person buying only water. Splitting the order into baskets lets the cashier serve quick customers in between.

How it works

async function processRows(rows) {
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
    process(rows[i]);
    if (i % 100 === 0) await yieldToBrowser();
  }
}

function yieldToBrowser() {
  // scheduler.yield() keeps your place in line (Chromium); setTimeout is the fallback
  return globalThis.scheduler?.yield ? scheduler.yield() : new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
}

Common traps

  • "Async functions don't block." The code between awaits still runs on the main thread. Only the waiting is offloaded.
  • INP vs FID. FID measured only the delay before the first input was handled. INP measures the whole response (delay + processing + next paint) for interactions throughout the visit.
  • Huge React renders count too. A state update that re-renders 5,000 rows is a long task: memoise, virtualise, or use transitions.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record while clicking around. Long tasks have a red triangle in the corner. The Interactions track shows how long each tap took to paint.

Quick quiz

What counts as a long task?

Any task that occupies the main thread for more than 50 ms.

What does INP measure?

The time from a user interaction (tap, click, keypress) until the next frame is painted, reported as roughly the worst interaction during the page visit. Good is 200 ms or less.

Three ways to fix a long task?

Chunk and yield (setTimeout / scheduler.yield), move work to a Web Worker, or reduce the work (virtualise lists, debounce, do it on the server).

title: Bubbling & capturing
text: Phases: capture ↓ → target → bubble ↑. Listeners default to bubble; { capture: true } for capture. stopPropagation (stop the journey) ≠ preventDefault (stop default action). target = clicked element, currentTarget = element whose listener runs. focus/blur/mouseenter/mouseleave don't bubble.
html:
• Phases: capture ↓ → target → bubble ↑. Listeners default to bubble; { capture: true } for capture.
  • stopPropagation (stop the journey) ≠ preventDefault (stop default action).
  • target = clicked element, currentTarget = element whose listener runs. focus/blur/mouseenter/mouseleave don't bubble.
deep_html:
Key points

  • A click travels in three phases: capture (down from window to the target), target, bubble (back up to window).
  • Listeners run in the bubble phase by default. Pass { capture: true } to run on the way down.
  • stopPropagation() stops the journey. preventDefault() stops the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form). They're different things.

Interview answer

DOM events propagate in three phases: capturing from the window down to the target's parent, the target phase, then bubbling back up to the window. addEventListener listens in the bubble phase by default, or capture if you pass capture: true. event.target is the element that was actually clicked, while event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running. stopPropagation stops further propagation; preventDefault cancels the default browser behaviour, and you can use either independently.

The analogy

A letter delivered to a flat. It goes down from the city post office to the building to the floor to your door (capture). You open it (target). Then the news spreads up: your floor hears, then the building, then the city (bubble). Anyone along the way can react, or stop the news from spreading further.

How it works

list.addEventListener('click', e => {
  console.log(e.target);         // the <button> you clicked (deepest element)
  console.log(e.currentTarget);  // the <ul> this listener is attached to
});

link.addEventListener('click', e => {
  e.preventDefault();      // don't navigate
  e.stopPropagation();     // and don't let parents hear about it
});

Common traps

  • target vs currentTarget. Mixing them up is the #1 bug in delegated handlers.
  • Not every event bubbles. focus, blur, mouseenter and mouseleave don't. Use focusin/focusout and mouseover/mouseout if you need bubbling.
  • stopPropagation breaks other code. Analytics, dropdown "click outside" handlers and delegation on parents stop working. Use it rarely.

See it yourself

DevTools → Elements → select an element → Event Listeners tab → tick Ancestors to see every listener that will hear a click on it.

Quick quiz

A div has a capture listener and its child button has a normal listener. Which runs first when you click the button?

The div's capture listener: capture runs on the way down, before the target and bubble phases.

Difference between stopPropagation and preventDefault?

stopPropagation stops the event from reaching other elements; preventDefault stops the browser's default action. A link click with preventDefault still bubbles.

Which common events don't bubble?

focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave (also load and scroll on elements).

title: Event delegation
text: One listener on the parent + e.target.closest('.row') . Fewer listeners, works for rows added later, no listener leaks. DevTools → Event Listeners → Ancestors. Trap: needs bubbling events; a child's stopPropagation hides it.
html:
• One listener on the parent + e.target.closest('.row').
  • Fewer listeners, works for rows added later, no listener leaks. DevTools → Event Listeners → Ancestors.
  • Trap: needs bubbling events; a child's stopPropagation hides it.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Event delegation: put one listener on a parent instead of one on every child. Use e.target.closest(...) to find which child was clicked.
  • It works for children added later, uses fewer listeners, and avoids leaks when items are removed.
  • It relies on bubbling, so it doesn't work with events that don't bubble, or if a child calls stopPropagation().

Interview answer

Event delegation means attaching a single listener to a common ancestor and using event bubbling to handle events from its descendants. Inside the handler I use event.target.closest with a selector to find the relevant child and check that it's inside the container. This reduces the number of listeners, automatically handles dynamically added elements, and avoids cleanup issues. It doesn't work for non-bubbling events like focus, where I'd use focusin instead.

The analogy

A class with 60 students. Instead of giving each student their own phone to call the teacher (60 listeners), there's one receptionist at the door who hears everyone and checks the name tag: "Ah, that's Riya from row 3."

How it works

const list = document.querySelector('#todo-list');

list.addEventListener('click', e => {
  const row = e.target.closest('.todo');      // walk up from what was clicked
  if (!row || !list.contains(row)) return;    // clicked empty space or outside

  if (e.target.closest('.delete')) row.remove();
  else row.classList.toggle('done');
});

// Rows added later work automatically
list.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '<li class="todo">New task <button class="delete">✕</button></li>');
  • React already does this for you: it attaches one listener per event type at the root and dispatches to your components.

Common traps

  • Using e.target directly. If the row contains a <span> or icon, e.target is that inner element. Always use closest().
  • Non-bubbling events. focus/blur won't reach the parent; use focusin/focusout.
  • A child's stopPropagation() means the parent never hears the click, so the delegated handler silently doesn't run.

See it yourself

DevTools → Elements → select a row → Event Listeners → tick Ancestors: on a delegated list you'll see one click listener on the parent, none on each row.

Quick quiz

Why use closest() instead of checking e.target.classList?

The click may land on a nested element (icon, span). closest() walks up from the clicked element to the nearest matching ancestor, so it finds the row either way.

Why does delegation work for elements added after page load?

The listener is on the parent, which already exists. Clicks on new children bubble up to it like any other.

When does delegation not work?

For events that don't bubble (focus, blur, mouseenter), or when something below calls stopPropagation.

title: Memory leaks
text: GC frees what's unreachable from roots; a leak is unneeded but still reachable memory. Suspects: listeners not removed, intervals after unmount, ever-growing caches, detached DOM nodes. Use useEffect cleanup, WeakMap. Memory panel: compare heap snapshots, filter "Detached". Closures keep captured variables alive.
html:
• GC frees what's unreachable from roots; a leak is unneeded but still reachable memory.
  • Suspects: listeners not removed, intervals after unmount, ever-growing caches, detached DOM nodes. Use useEffect cleanup, WeakMap.
  • Memory panel: compare heap snapshots, filter "Detached". Closures keep captured variables alive.
deep_html:
Key points

  • JavaScript frees memory automatically with garbage collection (GC): anything that can no longer be reached from the "roots" (globals, the current stack) is removed.
  • A memory leak is memory you don't need anymore but that's still reachable, so GC can't free it.
  • Usual suspects: listeners not removed, intervals still running, caches that only grow, detached DOM nodes, closures holding big data.

Interview answer

JavaScript uses mark-and-sweep garbage collection: starting from roots like the global object and the call stack, it marks everything reachable and frees the rest. A leak happens when something unneeded stays reachable, typically an event listener or interval that's never cleaned up, a global or module-level cache that keeps growing, or a closure or data structure that still references removed DOM nodes. In React I clean up subscriptions and timers in the useEffect cleanup function, and I find leaks by comparing heap snapshots in the Memory panel.

The analogy

A hotel that checks out guests automatically when nobody has their room key anymore. A leak is a guest who left the city but whose key is still on the reception desk: the room stays booked forever.

How it works

// Bad: Leaks: interval + listener keep running after the component unmounts
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(poll, 1000);
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
}, []);

// Good: Cleanup function removes them
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(poll, 1000);
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
  return () => {
    clearInterval(id);
    window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
  };
}, []);
  • Detached DOM nodes: removed from the page but still referenced from a JS variable or array, so the whole subtree stays in memory.
  • WeakMap/WeakRef hold keys without preventing their collection: handy for caches attached to objects.

Common traps

  • "JS has GC, so there are no leaks." GC only frees unreachable memory. Leaks are reachable by mistake.
  • Anonymous listeners can't be removed. removeEventListener needs the exact same function reference.
  • Closures keep their outer variables alive. A tiny callback can keep a huge array in memory.

See it yourself

DevTools → Memory → take a heap snapshot, use the page (open/close a modal 10 times), take another → choose Comparison. Filter by "Detached" to find removed DOM nodes that are still held.

Quick quiz

Why might a removed DOM element still use memory?

Some JS reference (a variable, array, cache, closure or listener) still points to it, so it's reachable and the GC can't free it: a detached DOM node.

What should a React useEffect cleanup do?

Undo everything the effect set up: clear timers, remove listeners, unsubscribe, abort fetches.

When is a WeakMap useful?

To associate data with objects (like DOM nodes) without keeping them alive: when the object is gone, its entry can be garbage-collected.

title: Observers
text: IntersectionObserver (lazy load, infinite scroll, autoplay, impressions), ResizeObserver, MutationObserver, PerformanceObserver. Better than scroll listeners: browser computes intersections, no forced layout in your code, fires only on threshold crossings.
html:
• IntersectionObserver (lazy load, infinite scroll, autoplay, impressions), ResizeObserver, MutationObserver, PerformanceObserver.
  • Better than scroll listeners: browser computes intersections, no forced layout in your code, fires only on threshold crossings.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Observers let the browser tell you when something happens, instead of you checking over and over.
  • IntersectionObserver: "this element entered or left the screen" (lazy loading, infinite scroll, autoplay, ad impressions).
  • ResizeObserver (an element's size changed), MutationObserver (the DOM changed), PerformanceObserver (performance entries like long tasks and layout shifts).

Interview answer

Instead of polling or listening to scroll and resize and measuring elements myself, which forces layout on the main thread, I use observers. IntersectionObserver reports when an element crosses a visibility threshold relative to the viewport or a root, which is ideal for lazy loading and infinite scroll. ResizeObserver reports element size changes, MutationObserver reports DOM changes, and PerformanceObserver streams performance entries. They're efficient because the browser computes the information during its own rendering work and only calls you when something actually changes.

The analogy

Instead of asking "are we there yet?" every 5 seconds (a scroll listener running getBoundingClientRect()), you ask the driver to tap you when we reach the exit. The driver already knows where the car is; you only get interrupted when it matters.

How it works

// Lazy-load images when they come within 200px of the screen
const io = new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    if (!entry.isIntersecting) continue;
    const img = entry.target;
    img.src = img.dataset.src;
    io.unobserve(img);              // done with this one
  }
}, { rootMargin: '200px' });

document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]').forEach(img => io.observe(img));

// Infinite scroll: load more when the sentinel at the bottom appears
new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => e.isIntersecting && loadMore())
  .observe(document.querySelector('#sentinel'));

Common traps

  • Forgetting to disconnect. Call unobserve() or disconnect() when done, or on unmount, to avoid leaks.
  • Native lazy loading exists. For simple images, <img loading="lazy"> is enough. Use IntersectionObserver for custom behaviour.
  • MutationObserver callbacks are batched microtasks, not synchronous per change.

See it yourself

Open a long page with many images, paste the lazy-load snippet into the Console (after changing a few src to data-src), and watch the Network tab: images load only as you scroll near them.

Quick quiz

Why is IntersectionObserver better than a scroll listener for lazy loading?

It fires only when visibility crosses a threshold, and the browser computes intersections itself, so your code doesn't run on every scroll or force layout with getBoundingClientRect.

What does rootMargin do?

It grows or shrinks the root's box, e.g. '200px' triggers the callback 200 px before the element actually enters the viewport, so content is ready in time.

Which observer would you use to react to an element's width changing (not the window's)?

ResizeObserver.

title: White screen first
text: Every strategy answers one question: who builds the HTML, and when? Server (before sending) or browser (after arriving). Server-rendered: HTML has content → paint now, JS later. Client-rendered: empty HTML → download JS → run → fetch → paint. See it: DevTools → Performance → ✓ Screenshots, Network = Slow 4G → reload → filmstrip. Trap: a white screen isn't always the network. Big bundles take seconds to parse/run on cheap CPUs → throttle CPU (4x) too.
html:
• Every strategy answers one question: who builds the HTML, and when? Server (before sending) or browser (after arriving).
  • Server-rendered: HTML has content → paint now, JS later. Client-rendered: empty HTML → download JS → run → fetch → paint.
  • See it: DevTools → Performance → ✓ Screenshots, Network = Slow 4G → reload → filmstrip.
  • Trap: a white screen isn't always the network. Big bundles take seconds to parse/run on cheap CPUs → throttle CPU (4x) too.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Every rendering strategy answers one question: who builds the HTML, and when?
  • Server-rendered: the HTML arrives with content, so the browser can paint right away. JS comes later.
  • Client-rendered: the HTML arrives nearly empty. The browser must download JS, run it, fetch data, then paint. Until then: white screen.

Interview answer

The core difference between rendering strategies is where and when HTML is produced. With server rendering, the server sends meaningful HTML so the first paint happens as soon as it arrives, and JavaScript hydrates it later. With client rendering, the server sends a shell and a bundle, and the user sees nothing useful until the JS downloads, parses, executes and fetches data. On slow phones that JS cost, not just the network, is often what causes the white screen.

The analogy

Ordering furniture. Server-rendered = it arrives assembled; you can sit on it immediately. Client-rendered = a flat-pack box arrives and you must assemble it before anyone can sit. Fast delivery doesn't help if assembly takes ages.

How it works

  • On a cheap Android phone, parsing and running 1 MB of JS can take several seconds even after it's downloaded.

Common traps

  • "White screen = slow network." Often it's the CPU. Throttle the CPU (4x slowdown) in DevTools, not just the network.
  • One strategy for the whole app. Different pages can use different strategies (later episodes).
  • "Server rendering means no JavaScript." Usually the same JS still loads to make the page interactive.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → tick Screenshots, set Network to Slow 4G and CPU to 4x slowdown → reload. The filmstrip shows exactly how long the screen stays white.

Quick quiz

What question does every rendering strategy answer?

Who builds the HTML (server or browser) and when (at build time, per request, or after the page loads).

Why can a client-rendered app show a white screen on a fast network?

The JS still has to be parsed and executed, then data fetched, before anything renders. On slow CPUs that takes seconds.

What does server rendering improve, and what doesn't it?

It improves first paint (content visible sooner). It doesn't remove the JS cost of making the page interactive.

title: Client-side rendering (CSR)
text:
Server sends
+ a bundle; JS builds the DOM in the browser. View Source = what the server sent (empty). Elements = live DOM after JS (full). static hosting, instant after first load. − slow first paint, crawlers/previews without JS see nothing. Trap: Google can render JS (sometimes deferred), but WhatsApp/LinkedIn link previews read raw HTML → blank preview.
html:
• Server sends <div id="root"></div> + a bundle; JS builds the DOM in the browser.
  • View Source = what the server sent (empty). Elements = live DOM after JS (full).
    • static hosting, instant after first load. − slow first paint, crawlers/previews without JS see nothing.
  • Trap: Google can render JS (sometimes deferred), but WhatsApp/LinkedIn link previews read raw HTML → blank preview.
deep_html:
Key points

  • In client-side rendering (CSR), the server sends an almost empty HTML file plus a JS bundle. JavaScript builds the whole page in the browser.
  • Pros: cheap static hosting, very fast navigation after the first load (feels like an app).
  • Cons: slow first paint, and tools that don't run JS (link previews, some crawlers) see a blank page.

Interview answer

In CSR the server returns a minimal HTML shell with a root element and script tags. The browser downloads and executes the bundle, which fetches data and renders the UI into the DOM. It's simple to host on a CDN and great for app-like experiences after load, but first contentful paint is slow, especially on low-end devices, and anything that reads raw HTML, like social link previews, sees no content. It fits dashboards and logged-in tools more than public, SEO-sensitive pages.

The analogy

A restaurant that hands you raw ingredients and a recipe card. Once you've learned the kitchen, cooking the next dish is quick. But the first meal takes a long time, and anyone peeking through the window just sees an empty table.

How it works

<!-- What the server actually sends in a CSR app -->
<body>
  <div id="root"></div>
  <script src="/assets/main.4f2a.js"></script>
</body>

Common traps

  • SEO and link previews. Google can run JS (sometimes later), but WhatsApp, LinkedIn and Slack previews read raw HTML only, so they show a blank card.
  • Loading spinners everywhere. Every page that fetches after render shows a spinner first; consider skeletons or prefetching.
  • Bundle growth. One big bundle makes every first visit slower. Split code by route.

See it yourself

On any React app built with Vite or Create React App: View Page Source shows an empty #root. DevTools → Elements shows the full page that JS built.

Quick quiz

Why does a CSR page's link preview show nothing?

Preview bots fetch the HTML without running JavaScript, and CSR HTML has no content, only an empty root element.

When is CSR a good choice?

Logged-in, highly interactive apps (dashboards, editors, internal tools) where SEO doesn't matter and users stay for long sessions.

View Source vs Elements panel: what's the difference in a CSR app?

View Source shows what the server sent (an empty shell). Elements shows the live DOM after JavaScript rendered the page.

title: Client-side routing
text: JS intercepts link clicks, history.pushState() updates the URL, fetches data, swaps part of the page. popstate = Back button. See it: YouTube → Network → Doc filter: no new document on video click; Fetch/XHR shows JSON ( next?… , player?… ). Trap: refreshing /products/42 → 404, because the server only has index.html . Fix: rewrite all routes to index.html ( try_files $uri /index.html; ).
html:
• JS intercepts link clicks, history.pushState() updates the URL, fetches data, swaps part of the page. popstate = Back button.
  • See it: YouTube → Network → Doc filter: no new document on video click; Fetch/XHR shows JSON (next?…, player?…).
  • Trap: refreshing /products/42 → 404, because the server only has index.html. Fix: rewrite all routes to index.html (try_files $uri /index.html;).
deep_html:
Key points

  • Client-side routing: JavaScript intercepts link clicks, changes the URL with history.pushState(), fetches data and swaps only part of the page. No full page reload.
  • The Back button fires a popstate event, which the router handles.
  • Refreshing a deep URL (/products/42) can 404 if the server isn't told to serve index.html for every route.

Interview answer

A client-side router listens for link clicks, prevents the browser's default navigation, and updates the URL using the History API's pushState. It then renders the matching component and fetches only the data it needs, so the page doesn't reload. Back and forward trigger popstate, which the router uses to render the previous route. Because the server only knows index.html, it must be configured to return index.html for all app routes, otherwise a refresh on a nested URL returns 404.

The analogy

A mall map screen. Tapping a shop doesn't send you to a new building; the same screen just redraws the map for that shop. But if someone gives a visitor the address "Shop 42" directly, the security guard (the server) must know to send them to the map screen, not say "no such building".

How it works

// The core of every router, in a few lines
document.addEventListener('click', e => {
  const a = e.target.closest('a[data-link]');
  if (!a) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  history.pushState({}, '', a.href);
  render(location.pathname);
});
window.addEventListener('popstate', () => render(location.pathname));

# Server: send index.html for any route the files don't match
location / { try_files $uri /index.html; }

Common traps

  • The refresh 404. Fix it with a rewrite rule (Nginx try_files, Netlify /* /index.html 200).
  • Scroll position and focus. A router must restore scroll on Back and move focus for screen-reader users.
  • Hash routing (/#/page) avoids the server issue but looks dated and is worse for SEO.

See it yourself

Open YouTube → DevTools → Network → filter Doc. Click a video: no new document loads; filter Fetch/XHR and you'll see JSON requests instead.

Quick quiz

Which browser API lets you change the URL without reloading?

The History API: history.pushState() (and replaceState()).

Why does refreshing /products/42 give a 404 on some SPAs?

The server looks for a real file at that path and doesn't find one. It must be configured to serve index.html for all app routes.
