What event fires when the user presses Back?

popstate.

title: Server-side rendering (SSR)
text: Every request: server fetches data + builds full HTML → browser paints immediately; JS loads after to make it interactive. TTFB goes up (server is cooking), first paint comes sooner. See it: View Source on Amazon shows titles/prices; Network → document → Timing → "Waiting for server response" ≈ render time. Trap: SSR isn't always faster — slow DB or far server = huge TTFB, and still not interactive until JS. SSR moves work, doesn't delete it.
html:
• Every request: server fetches data + builds full HTML → browser paints immediately; JS loads after to make it interactive.
  • TTFB goes up (server is cooking), first paint comes sooner.
  • See it: View Source on Amazon shows titles/prices; Network → document → Timing → "Waiting for server response" ≈ render time.
  • Trap: SSR isn't always faster — slow DB or far server = huge TTFB, and still not interactive until JS. SSR moves work, doesn't delete it.
deep_html:
Key points

  • In server-side rendering (SSR), the server fetches data and builds the full HTML on every request.
  • The browser paints content immediately; JavaScript then loads and makes the page interactive (hydration).
  • Trade-off: first paint comes sooner, but TTFB (time to first byte) goes up because the server is doing work before responding.

Interview answer

With SSR, each request runs the app on the server: it fetches the data, renders components to HTML and sends a complete page. The user sees content as soon as the HTML arrives, which helps first contentful paint and SEO, and then the client bundle hydrates the page to make it interactive. The cost is higher server load and TTFB, since nothing is sent until rendering finishes, and the page still isn't interactive until hydration completes.

The analogy

A restaurant that cooks your dish fresh when you order. You wait a bit longer before the plate arrives (TTFB), but it arrives ready to eat, unlike the flat-pack kitchen of CSR.

How it works

// Next.js (App Router): this component runs on the server for each request
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';
export default async function Product({ params }) {
  const product = await db.product.find(params.id);
  return <h1>{product.title} · ₹{product.price}</h1>;
}

Common traps

  • "SSR is always faster." A slow database or a far-away server makes TTFB huge, and the page can feel slower than CSR.
  • SSR doesn't delete JavaScript. The page still needs the bundle to hydrate before clicks work.
  • Caching matters. Rendering the same page for every visitor is wasted work; cache it or use SSG/ISR where possible.

See it yourself

View Source on an Amazon product page: titles and prices are in the HTML. DevTools → Network → the document request → Timing → "Waiting for server response" roughly equals server render time.

Quick quiz

Which metric gets worse with SSR, and which gets better?

TTFB usually gets worse (the server renders first). First contentful paint usually gets better (HTML arrives with content).

Is an SSR page interactive as soon as it's visible?

No. It becomes interactive only after the JavaScript downloads and hydration attaches event handlers.

When would you choose SSR over SSG?

When the content is personalised or changes per request (user-specific pages, live prices, search results) and must still be visible quickly and crawlable.

title: Static site generation (SSG)
text: HTML built once at build time , copied to CDN edges, served as-is. Great for docs, blogs, marketing. Headers: cache HIT, large age → built long before you asked. Trap: 50k products + hourly prices → slow builds + stale until next deploy. Not on its own.
html:
• HTML built once at build time, copied to CDN edges, served as-is. Great for docs, blogs, marketing.
  • Headers: cache HIT, large age → built long before you asked.
  • Trap: 50k products + hourly prices → slow builds + stale until next deploy. Not on its own.
deep_html:
Key points

  • In static site generation (SSG), HTML is built once, at build time, then copied to CDN servers worldwide.
  • Every visitor gets the same ready-made file, so it's the fastest and cheapest option.
  • Perfect for content that rarely changes: docs, blogs, marketing pages. Bad on its own for data that changes often.

Interview answer

SSG renders pages to HTML during the build step, not per request. Those files are deployed to a CDN and served directly, so TTFB is minimal, there's no server rendering cost, and it scales to any traffic. The limitation is freshness: content only changes when you rebuild and redeploy, and build time grows with the number of pages, so it suits docs, blogs and marketing sites rather than large catalogues with frequently changing data.

The analogy

Printing newspapers overnight. Everyone in the morning gets an identical copy instantly. But if a price changes at 10 AM, the paper is wrong until tomorrow's print run.

How it works

// Next.js: generate one static page per blog post at build time
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await getAllPosts();
  return posts.map(p => ({ slug: p.slug }));
}

Common traps

  • 50,000 products with hourly price changes. Builds take too long and data is stale between deploys. Use ISR or SSR for those.
  • Personalised content. Static HTML is the same for everyone. Add personal bits on the client (e.g. "Hi, Riya").
  • Forgetting it can still be interactive. Static HTML can hydrate interactive components like any other page.

See it yourself

Open a docs site (e.g. a Next.js or Astro docs page) → DevTools → Network → document → Headers: a cache HIT and a large age value show it was built long before you asked.

Quick quiz

When is the HTML generated in SSG?

At build time, once, before any visitor requests the page.

Why is SSG so fast?

The page is a pre-built file served from a CDN edge near the user: no server rendering or database work per request.

What's SSG's main weakness?

Freshness and build time: content changes require a rebuild, which gets slow with many pages.

title: Incremental static regeneration (ISR)
text: Static page + expiry. After it expires, the next visitor still gets the old page; a rebuild of that page runs in the background. Next.js: export const revalidate = 60; · on-demand: revalidatePath('/product/42') . Same idea in HTTP: Cache-Control: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate . Trap: the first visitor after expiry still sees the OLD page; pages nobody visits stay stale.
html:
• Static page + expiry. After it expires, the next visitor still gets the old page; a rebuild of that page runs in the background.
  • Next.js: export const revalidate = 60; · on-demand: revalidatePath('/product/42').
  • Same idea in HTTP: Cache-Control: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate.
  • Trap: the first visitor after expiry still sees the OLD page; pages nobody visits stay stale.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) = a static page with an expiry time.
  • After it expires, the next visitor still gets the old page instantly, while that one page is rebuilt in the background.
  • Everyone after that gets the fresh version. It's static speed with data that stays reasonably current.

Interview answer

ISR serves pre-rendered static pages from a cache, but each page has a revalidation window. When a request comes in after the window has passed, the cached page is still served immediately, and a background regeneration is triggered for that page only. Once it succeeds, the cache is updated for subsequent visitors. It's the stale-while-revalidate idea applied to pages, and frameworks also support on-demand revalidation when you know data has changed.

The analogy

A café's daily specials board. The board is rewritten only when it's out of date, and only after the first customer of the day notices. That customer still reads yesterday's board, but the staff update it right away for everyone after.

How it works

// Next.js: rebuild this page at most once a minute
export const revalidate = 60;

// Or on demand, e.g. after an admin edits a product
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
revalidatePath('/product/42');

# Same idea at the HTTP/CDN level
Cache-Control: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

Common traps

  • The first visitor after expiry sees stale data. It's "eventually fresh", not real-time. Don't use it for stock counts at checkout.
  • Pages nobody visits stay stale because regeneration is triggered by a request.
  • Choosing the window. Too short = lots of rebuilds; too long = stale content. Prefer on-demand revalidation when you can.

See it yourself

Deploy a Next.js page with revalidate = 10 that prints the time. Refresh after 10 s: you see the old time once, then the new time on the next refresh.

Quick quiz

After the revalidate time passes, what does the next visitor see?

The old cached page, immediately. A rebuild starts in the background for later visitors.

What's the HTTP equivalent of ISR?

Cache-Control: s-maxage=…, stale-while-revalidate=… on a CDN.

How can you update a page right after data changes instead of waiting?

On-demand revalidation, e.g. revalidatePath() or revalidateTag() called from a webhook or admin action.

title: Hydration
text: Server HTML = a picture. Hydration = React re-runs components in the browser and attaches handlers to the existing DOM. renderToString(<App />) on the server · hydrateRoot(root, <App />) in the browser. Runs on the main thread → one long task; taps wait. Trap: it does NOT rebuild the DOM, but it DOES run every component again → CPU cost.
html:
• Server HTML = a picture. Hydration = React re-runs components in the browser and attaches handlers to the existing DOM.
  • renderToString(<App />) on the server · hydrateRoot(root, <App />) in the browser.
  • Runs on the main thread → one long task; taps wait.
  • Trap: it does NOT rebuild the DOM, but it DOES run every component again → CPU cost.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Server HTML is like a picture of the page: it looks right, but buttons don't work yet.
  • Hydration = React runs your components again in the browser and attaches event handlers to the existing DOM (it doesn't rebuild it).
  • It runs on the main thread, often as one long task, so taps during hydration wait.

Interview answer

After server rendering, the browser has static HTML but no event listeners or component state. Hydration loads the same component code on the client, renders the tree in memory, matches it against the existing DOM, and attaches event handlers and state instead of recreating nodes. It's called with hydrateRoot. Because it re-executes every component, it costs CPU time on the main thread, which delays interactivity on slow devices.

The analogy

Adding water to instant noodles. The noodles (HTML) are already there and look like food, but you can't eat them until you add hot water (JavaScript) and wait.

How it works

// server.js
import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server';
const html = renderToString(<App />);

// client.js
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
hydrateRoot(document.getElementById('root'), <App />);

Common traps

  • "Hydration rebuilds the DOM." It reuses the existing DOM; it does re-run every component, which is the expensive part.
  • createRoot instead of hydrateRoot throws away the server HTML and re-renders from scratch.
  • Bigger trees = longer hydration. Fewer client components means less to hydrate.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance with CPU 4x slowdown → reload an SSR site → look for a big scripting block after the first paint: that's hydration.

Quick quiz

What does hydration actually do?

Re-runs components on the client to rebuild React's internal tree and attach event listeners and state to the server-rendered DOM.

Why can taps feel ignored right after an SSR page appears?

Hydration hasn't finished: there are no handlers yet, and the main thread may be busy hydrating.

Which React API hydrates a server-rendered root?

hydrateRoot from react-dom/client.

title: Hydration mismatch
text:
Rule: server HTML must equal the browser's first render. Causes: Date , Math.random() , window / localStorage in render, timezone/locale, invalid nesting (
in

), extensions. Fix: same placeholder on both sides → fill browser-only values in useEffect . Tiny diffs: suppressHydrationWarning . Trap: typeof window checks in render CAUSE mismatches.
html:
• Rule: server HTML must equal the browser's first render.
  • Causes: Date, Math.random(), window/localStorage in render, timezone/locale, invalid nesting (<div> in <p>), extensions.
  • Fix: same placeholder on both sides → fill browser-only values in useEffect. Tiny diffs: suppressHydrationWarning.
  • Trap: typeof window checks in render CAUSE mismatches.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Hydration has one rule: the server's HTML must match the browser's first render.
  • Mismatches come from values that differ between server and browser: Date, Math.random(), window/localStorage, timezone or locale, invalid HTML nesting, browser extensions.
  • Fix: render the same placeholder on both sides, then fill browser-only values in useEffect.

Interview answer

A hydration mismatch happens when the HTML generated on the server differs from what the client renders on its first pass. Common causes are time and random values, reading browser-only APIs like window or localStorage during render, locale and timezone formatting, and invalid nesting that the browser repairs. React warns and may re-render that subtree on the client. The fix is to make the initial render deterministic, then update browser-specific values in an effect after hydration.

The analogy

Two people assembling the same flat-pack with different manuals. When they compare, the pieces don't line up, and one of them has to take it apart and redo it.

How it works

function LocalTime() {
  const [time, setTime] = useState(null);           // same on server and client
  useEffect(() => setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()), []);
  return <span>{time ?? '--:--'}</span>;
}

Common traps

  • typeof window checks in render cause mismatches: the server renders one thing, the browser another.
  • suppressHydrationWarning is only for tiny, expected differences (like a timestamp), not a general fix.
  • Browser extensions that inject DOM can trigger warnings you can't reproduce in incognito.

See it yourself

In a Next.js or Remix app, render new Date().toISOString() directly in a component and reload: the console shows a hydration error pointing at the text.

Quick quiz

Why does `Math.random()` in render cause a mismatch?

The server and browser each generate a different number, so the first client render doesn't match the server HTML.

How do you safely show something that depends on localStorage?

Render a neutral placeholder first, then read localStorage in useEffect and update state after hydration.

Can invalid HTML cause hydration errors?

Yes. The browser repairs invalid nesting (like a div inside a p) when parsing, so the DOM no longer matches what React expects.

title: Visible but not clickable
text: The uncanny valley: visible (FCP) but not interactive (JS loading/hydrating). FCP = first see something · TTI = reliably responds · TBT = blocked time in between. Field: INP. See it: Performance, CPU 4x slowdown → gap between first content screenshot and end of long tasks. Trap: green Lighthouse (one lab device) ≠ real users on cheap phones → check field INP.
html:
• The uncanny valley: visible (FCP) but not interactive (JS loading/hydrating).
  • FCP = first see something · TTI = reliably responds · TBT = blocked time in between. Field: INP.
  • See it: Performance, CPU 4x slowdown → gap between first content screenshot and end of long tasks.
  • Trap: green Lighthouse (one lab device) ≠ real users on cheap phones → check field INP.
deep_html:
Key points

  • The uncanny valley: the page is visible but not yet interactive because JS is still loading or hydrating.
  • FCP = first time you see something. TTI = when it reliably responds. TBT = how long the main thread was blocked in between.
  • In the field, this shows up as bad INP (slow response to taps).

Interview answer

With SSR the page can paint early, but it isn't usable until JavaScript has downloaded and hydrated. That gap between First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive is where users tap and nothing happens, which is frustrating and causes rage clicks. In lab tools it shows as high Total Blocking Time; in real-user data it appears as poor INP. Reducing JavaScript, splitting hydration, and deferring non-critical scripts shrink that gap.

The analogy

A shop with the lights on and products on display, but the doors are still locked. People can see everything and keep pushing the door.

How it works

  • Lab metric to watch: Total Blocking Time (time above 50 ms in each long task between FCP and TTI).
  • Field metric to watch: INP, since that's what real users experience.

Common traps

  • Green Lighthouse score ≠ happy users. Lighthouse tests one simulated device; real users on cheap phones may have much worse INP.
  • Showing buttons before they work with no feedback. Consider disabled states or making critical forms work without JS.
  • Third-party scripts (chat widgets, analytics) often cause the biggest long tasks.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → CPU 4x slowdown → reload with Screenshots on. Compare the first screenshot with content to where the long tasks end: that's your uncanny valley.

Quick quiz

What's the difference between FCP and TTI?

FCP is when content first appears; TTI is when the page reliably responds to input. The gap between them is the uncanny valley.

What does Total Blocking Time measure?

The sum of the portions of long tasks over 50 ms between FCP and TTI: how long input would have been blocked.

Which Core Web Vital reflects this problem for real users?

INP (Interaction to Next Paint).

title: Selective hydration
text: Classic hydration is all-or-nothing. React 18 hydrates each <Suspense> boundary independently, yielding between chunks. Clicking an un-hydrated part → React hydrates it first, then replays the click. Trap: it doesn't make JS smaller — same code downloads and runs; only order + chunking change.
html:
• Classic hydration is all-or-nothing. React 18 hydrates each <Suspense> boundary independently, yielding between chunks.
  • Clicking an un-hydrated part → React hydrates it first, then replays the click.
  • Trap: it doesn't make JS smaller — same code downloads and runs; only order + chunking change.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Classic hydration is all or nothing: the whole page hydrates in one go before anything works.
  • With React 18+, each <Suspense> boundary hydrates on its own, and React yields to the browser between chunks.
  • If you click a part that isn't hydrated yet, React hydrates that part first, then replays your click.

Interview answer

React 18 introduced selective hydration. When the page is wrapped in Suspense boundaries, React can hydrate each boundary independently instead of the whole tree at once, and it yields between them so the browser can handle input. If the user interacts with a boundary that hasn't hydrated, React prioritises it and replays the event afterwards. It improves responsiveness, but it doesn't reduce the total JavaScript that's downloaded and executed.

The analogy

Opening a big store floor by floor instead of keeping the whole building shut until every floor is ready. If a customer walks up to the third floor first, staff rush to open that floor next.

How it works

<Layout>
  <Header />
  <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
    <Comments />          {/* hydrates independently */}
  </Suspense>
  <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
    <Recommendations />   {/* hydrates independently */}
  </Suspense>
</Layout>

Common traps

  • It doesn't make the JS smaller. The same code still downloads and runs; only the order and chunking change.
  • No boundaries = no benefit. Without Suspense boundaries, the tree still hydrates as one unit.
  • Too many tiny boundaries add overhead and can cause flickering fallbacks.

See it yourself

In a React 18 SSR app with Suspense around heavy sections, record Performance with CPU throttling: hydration appears as several smaller tasks instead of one long one.

Quick quiz

What unit does React hydrate independently?

Each Suspense boundary.

What happens if a user clicks an un-hydrated boundary?

React hydrates that boundary with priority, then replays the click event.

Does selective hydration reduce bundle size?

No. It changes when and in what order hydration work happens, not how much code is shipped.

title: Streaming SSR
text: Send the shell + fallbacks first; stream the slow parts later with a tiny script that swaps them in. React: renderToPipeableStream(<App />, { onShellReady() { stream.pipe(res) } }) . Works because HTTP bodies arrive in pieces (chunked in 1.1, DATA frames in 2/3). See it: Timing → long "Content Download"; View Source → <div hidden id="S:0"> + $RC(...) scripts. Trap: once the first chunk is out, status/headers are sent → no 404/redirect later. Decide before the shell.
html:
• Send the shell + fallbacks first; stream the slow parts later with a tiny script that swaps them in.
  • React: renderToPipeableStream(<App />, { onShellReady() { stream.pipe(res) } }).
  • Works because HTTP bodies arrive in pieces (chunked in 1.1, DATA frames in 2/3).
  • See it: Timing → long "Content Download"; View Source → <div hidden id="S:0"> + $RC(...) scripts.
  • Trap: once the first chunk is out, status/headers are sent → no 404/redirect later. Decide before the shell.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Streaming SSR sends the page in pieces: first the shell with loading placeholders, then each slow section as soon as its data is ready.
  • It works because HTTP responses can arrive in chunks; the browser renders as it goes.
  • A tiny inline script swaps each streamed section into its placeholder.

Interview answer

With streaming SSR the server doesn't wait for all data before responding. It flushes the HTML shell and Suspense fallbacks immediately, so the user sees layout and fast content early, then streams each boundary's HTML as its data resolves, along with a small script that moves it into place. In React this is renderToPipeableStream or the streaming APIs in frameworks like Next.js. The important caveat is that once the first bytes are sent, the status code and headers are fixed.

The analogy

A thali served one bowl at a time. Rice and dal arrive first so you can start eating; the dish that takes longest to cook is brought out when it's ready, into the empty space already on your plate.

How it works

// Node + React: send the shell as soon as it's ready
const { pipe } = renderToPipeableStream(<App />, {
  onShellReady() {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html');
    pipe(res);
  },
});

Common traps

  • Status codes are locked once streaming starts. You can't send a 404 or redirect after the shell is out, so decide those before the shell.
  • Buffering proxies (some CDNs, compression settings) can hold the whole response and kill streaming.
  • Fallback layout shift. Size your fallbacks like the final content to avoid CLS.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → the document → Timing: a long "Content Download" phase means it was streamed. View Source shows hidden <div hidden id="S:0"> chunks and small $RC(...) scripts at the bottom.

Quick quiz

What gets sent first in streaming SSR?

The shell: layout, fast content and Suspense fallbacks.

Why can't you return a 404 halfway through a streamed page?

Status and headers are sent with the first chunk; after that they can't be changed.

What makes streaming possible at the HTTP level?

Response bodies can arrive in pieces (chunked transfer in HTTP/1.1, DATA frames in HTTP/2 and 3), and browsers parse HTML incrementally.

title: React Server Components (RSC)
text: Run only on the server; can be async and read the DB; their code never ships. Only output (RSC payload) does. Interactive parts = 'use client' components; only those ship JS. See it: nextjs.org → Network → ?_rsc= requests on navigation. RSC ≠ SSR: SSR = HTML for first load, then everything hydrates. RSC never hydrates, refetchable on navigation. Frameworks use both. Trap: no useState / onClick in server components → pass data as props to a client component.
html:
• Run only on the server; can be async and read the DB; their code never ships. Only output (RSC payload) does.
  • Interactive parts = 'use client' components; only those ship JS.
  • See it: nextjs.org → Network → ?_rsc= requests on navigation.
  • RSC ≠ SSR: SSR = HTML for first load, then everything hydrates. RSC never hydrates, refetchable on navigation. Frameworks use both.
  • Trap: no useState/onClick in server components → pass data as props to a client component.
deep_html:
Key points

  • React Server Components (RSC) run only on the server. They can be async, read the database directly, and their code is never sent to the browser.
  • Only their output travels to the browser. Interactive parts are marked 'use client', and only those ship JavaScript.
  • RSC is not the same as SSR: SSR makes HTML for the first load, then everything hydrates. Server components never hydrate.

Interview answer

React Server Components are components that execute only on the server. They can fetch data directly and use server-only dependencies, and only their rendered result, the RSC payload, is sent to the client, so their code adds nothing to the bundle. Components that need state, effects or event handlers are client components marked with 'use client', and server components pass them data as props. SSR and RSC are complementary: frameworks render both to HTML for the first load, but only client components hydrate.

The analogy

A restaurant where some dishes are cooked in the kitchen and served ready (server components), while a few come with a DIY grill at your table (client components). You only pay for the grills you actually use.

How it works

// ProductPage.jsx: a server component (the default in Next.js App Router)
import AddToCart from './AddToCart';
export default async function ProductPage({ id }) {
  const product = await db.product.find(id);        // direct DB access
  return (<>
    <h1>{product.title}</h1>
    <AddToCart productId={id} />                     {/* only this ships JS */}
  </>);
}

// AddToCart.jsx
'use client';
export default function AddToCart({ productId }) {
  const [added, setAdded] = useState(false);
  return <button onClick={() => setAdded(true)}>{added ? 'Added' : 'Add to cart'}</button>;
}

Common traps

  • useState or onClick in a server component throws an error. Move the interactive bit into a client component.
  • Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable. No functions or class instances from server to client.
  • Importing a client component makes it a client boundary, including everything it imports.

See it yourself

Open nextjs.org → DevTools → Network → click between docs pages: requests with ?_rsc= carry the RSC payload instead of a full HTML page.

Quick quiz

Does a server component's code end up in the browser bundle?

No. Only its rendered output is sent.

How is RSC different from SSR?

SSR renders components to HTML for the initial load and then hydrates all of them. Server components run only on the server, never hydrate, and can be re-fetched on navigation.

How do you add a click handler to part of a server-rendered page?

Put that part in a client component marked 'use client' and pass it data as props.

title: Server Actions
text: 'use server' function called like a normal function → React sends a POST ( Next-Action: <id> header). Works with <form action={fn}> even before JS loads (progressive enhancement). Trap: it's a PUBLIC POST endpoint. Always check auth and validate inputs inside the action.
html:
• 'use server' function called like a normal function → React sends a POST (Next-Action: <id> header).
  • Works with <form action={fn}> even before JS loads (progressive enhancement).
  • Trap: it's a PUBLIC POST endpoint. Always check auth and validate inputs inside the action.
deep_html:
Key points

  • A Server Action is a function marked 'use server' that you call from the client like a normal function. React turns that call into a POST request to your server.
  • It works with <form action={fn}>, even before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement).
  • It's a public endpoint: always check auth and validate the input inside it.

Interview answer

Server Actions let you define server-side functions with 'use server' and call them directly from components or pass them to a form's action. Under the hood the framework creates an endpoint and sends a POST with an action ID and the serialized arguments, then returns the result and can revalidate cached data. Forms using actions work without client JavaScript. Because anyone can call that endpoint, the action must authenticate the user and validate every input, exactly like an API route.

The analogy

A hotel room phone with a "room service" button. You just press it; you don't need to know the kitchen's number or how the order travels. But the kitchen must still check that the order really comes from a guest.

How it works

// actions.js
'use server';
export async function createTodo(formData) {
  const user = await getUser();                 // auth check
  if (!user) throw new Error('Not signed in');
  const title = String(formData.get('title') ?? '').trim();
  if (!title || title.length > 200) return { error: 'Invalid title' };   // validate
  await db.todo.create({ title, userId: user.id });
  revalidatePath('/todos');
}

// TodoForm.jsx
import { createTodo } from './actions';
export default function TodoForm() {
  return <form action={createTodo}><input name="title" /><button>Add</button></form>;
}

Common traps

  • Trusting the caller. The action is reachable by anyone who sends the right POST. Check permissions every time.
  • Returning secrets. Whatever you return is sent to the browser.
  • Using actions for data fetching. They're for mutations; fetch data in server components.

See it yourself

In a Next.js app, submit a form that uses an action → DevTools → Network: a POST to the same page with a Next-Action header.

Quick quiz

What does calling a server action do at the network level?

The framework sends a POST request to the server with an action ID and serialized arguments, runs the function, and returns the result.

Why do forms with server actions work before JS loads?

The form posts natively using standard HTML form submission; JavaScript only enhances it.

What must every server action do?

Authenticate/authorize the user and validate inputs, because it's a public endpoint.

title: Islands architecture
text: Static HTML by default; only interactive widgets hydrate, each independently ( <astro-island> in Elements). Astro: client:load , client:visible (IntersectionObserver), client:idle . Trap: islands are separate apps → props can't cross. Share via a store (nanostores), custom events, or rethink boundaries.
html:
• Static HTML by default; only interactive widgets hydrate, each independently (<astro-island> in Elements).
  • Astro: client:load, client:visible (IntersectionObserver), client:idle.
  • Trap: islands are separate apps → props can't cross. Share via a store (nanostores), custom events, or rethink boundaries.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Islands architecture: the page is static HTML by default, and only the interactive widgets (a carousel, a cart button) ship JavaScript and hydrate.
  • Each island hydrates independently, and you choose when: on load, when visible, or when the browser is idle.
  • Astro popularised it: client:load, client:visible, client:idle.

Interview answer

In islands architecture most of the page is rendered to static HTML with no JavaScript, and only specific interactive components are hydrated as isolated islands. Each island loads its own JS and can be hydrated with different strategies, such as immediately, when idle, or when it scrolls into view using IntersectionObserver. This dramatically cuts JavaScript on content-heavy sites. The trade-off is that islands are separate apps, so sharing state between them needs a shared store or events.

The analogy

A museum where only a few exhibits are interactive touch screens. Most of the walls are just printed boards (static HTML). You only power the screens people actually use, when they walk up to them.

How it works

---
import Header from './Header.astro';      // static, no JS
import Carousel from './Carousel.jsx';
import Newsletter from './Newsletter.jsx';
---
<Header />
<Carousel client:visible />              <!-- hydrates when scrolled into view -->
<Newsletter client:idle />               <!-- hydrates when the browser is idle -->

Common traps

  • Islands can't share React state directly. Each is its own app. Use a small shared store (e.g. nanostores), custom events, or merge them into one island.
  • Too many islands each bring their framework runtime overhead.
  • Not a fit for app-like pages (dashboards) where almost everything is interactive.

See it yourself

Open an Astro site → DevTools → Elements: interactive parts are wrapped in <astro-island> tags with their hydration strategy as an attribute.

Quick quiz

What's the default for content in an islands architecture?

Static HTML with no JavaScript.

How does client:visible decide when to hydrate?

It uses IntersectionObserver and hydrates the island when it enters the viewport.

Two islands need the same cart count. What are your options?

A shared store both subscribe to, custom DOM events between them, or combining them into one island.

title: Resumability
text: Qwik: server serializes state + event wiring into HTML; browser resumes without re-running components. Handlers are URLs to small chunks ( on:click="q-…js#s_…" ); one tiny global listener loads code on interaction. Trap: first interaction must fetch code → slow on bad networks; mitigate by prefetching likely handlers.
html:
• Qwik: server serializes state + event wiring into HTML; browser resumes without re-running components.
  • Handlers are URLs to small chunks (on:click="q-…js#s_…"); one tiny global listener loads code on interaction.
  • Trap: first interaction must fetch code → slow on bad networks; mitigate by prefetching likely handlers.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Resumability (from the Qwik framework) skips hydration completely.
  • The server serialises the app's state and event wiring into the HTML. The browser resumes where the server stopped, without re-running components.
  • Event handlers are tiny chunks loaded only when the user interacts.

Interview answer

Hydration has to re-execute components on the client to rebuild state and attach listeners. Resumability avoids that: the server serializes application state and the location of each event handler into the HTML, and a tiny global listener on the client loads and runs only the specific handler chunk when an interaction occurs. Startup JavaScript is close to zero regardless of app size. The trade-off is that the first interaction may need to fetch code, so frameworks prefetch likely handlers.

The analogy

Pausing a video game and saving to a memory card. Resuming loads you right back to the same spot. You don't replay the whole level to get there, which is what hydration does.

How it works

<!-- Qwik output: the handler is a reference to a small lazy-loaded chunk -->
<button on:click="q-chunk-abc.js#s_onClickHandler">Add to cart</button>

Common traps

  • First click can be slow on a bad network because the handler code is fetched then. Prefetching (Qwik does this with a service worker) mitigates it.
  • Serialization limits: state must be serializable to go into the HTML.
  • It's not "no JavaScript". JS still runs; it's just loaded lazily, piece by piece.

See it yourself

Open a Qwik demo site → DevTools → Network (JS filter) → load the page: very little JS. Click a button and watch a small chunk load at that moment.

Quick quiz

What step does resumability skip?

Hydration, meaning re-executing components on the client to rebuild state and attach handlers.

Where does the app state live when the page loads?

Serialized inside the HTML sent by the server.

What's the main downside?

The first interaction may need to download its handler code, which is slow on poor networks unless prefetched.

title: Edge rendering
text: Run SSR in many small data centers near users (where CDNs live). Lighter runtimes: no full Node, small memory/CPU limits. Great for personalization, redirects, A/B tests, auth checks. Trap: edge render + single-region DB = every query crosses the planet. Only helps when data is close or cached.
html:
• Run SSR in many small data centers near users (where CDNs live). Lighter runtimes: no full Node, small memory/CPU limits.
  • Great for personalization, redirects, A/B tests, auth checks.
  • Trap: edge render + single-region DB = every query crosses the planet. Only helps when data is close or cached.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Edge rendering runs your server-side rendering in many small data centers close to users (the same places CDNs live).
  • Edge runtimes are lighter than Node: limited APIs, memory and CPU time.
  • Great for personalisation, redirects, A/B tests and auth checks. Useless if every render must query a database on the other side of the world.

Interview answer

Edge rendering executes server code in globally distributed locations near the user, typically on lightweight runtimes based on web standards rather than full Node.js. That cuts network latency for the request itself, which is great for redirects, geolocation, A/B testing, authentication and personalised responses. But if the edge function needs data from a database in a single region, every query travels back to that region, so the latency savings disappear. It works best with cached, replicated or edge-friendly data.

The analogy

Opening small kitchens in every neighbourhood. Delivery is faster, unless every kitchen still has to phone the central warehouse in another city for each ingredient.

How it works

// Next.js middleware runs at the edge: redirect by country before rendering
export function middleware(req) {
  const country = req.geo?.country;
  if (country === 'IN' && !req.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith('/in')) {
    return Response.redirect(new URL('/in' + req.nextUrl.pathname, req.url));
  }
}

Common traps

  • Edge function + far database = slower, not faster. Several sequential queries each cross the globe.
  • Node APIs missing. Some libraries (native modules, fs) don't work in edge runtimes.
  • Cold starts and limits vary by provider; heavy rendering may hit CPU time caps.

See it yourself

On a site deployed on Vercel or Cloudflare, check response headers like x-vercel-id or cf-ray: they include the edge location code that served you (e.g. bom for Mumbai).

Quick quiz

What does edge rendering mainly reduce?

Network latency between the user and the code handling their request.

When can edge rendering make a page slower?

When the render needs data from a database in one far-away region, so each query adds a long round trip.

Give three good edge use cases.

Redirects and rewrites, A/B test bucketing, auth/session checks, geolocation-based personalisation.

title: Case study: an online store
text: 3 questions per page: SEO? Same for everyone? How often does data change? /blog SSG · / ISR · /product/:id ISR + client islands (price/stock/cart) · /search streaming SSR · cart/checkout/account CSR. Trap: one strategy for the whole app. Choose per route, even per component.
html:
• 3 questions per page: SEO? Same for everyone? How often does data change?
  • /blog SSG · / ISR · /product/:id ISR + client islands (price/stock/cart) · /search streaming SSR · cart/checkout/account CSR.
  • Trap: one strategy for the whole app. Choose per route, even per component.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Pick a rendering strategy per page, not per app, by asking three questions: Does it need SEO? Is it the same for everyone? How often does the data change?
  • A typical online store mixes SSG, ISR, SSR, streaming and CSR on different routes.
  • Even within one page, static parts and live parts (price, stock, cart) can render differently.

Interview answer

I'd choose rendering per route based on SEO needs, personalisation and data freshness. Marketing and blog pages are static. The home page and product pages can be incrementally regenerated for speed and SEO, with live bits like stock, price and the add-to-cart button as client components. Search results are personalised and dynamic, so streaming SSR fits. Cart, checkout and account pages are private and highly interactive, so client rendering behind auth is fine. One strategy for everything always compromises somewhere.

The analogy

A restaurant doesn't cook everything the same way: bread is baked in the morning (SSG), curries are refreshed every few hours (ISR), dosas are made to order (SSR), and you mix your own salad at the table (CSR).

How it works

Common traps

  • One strategy for the whole app. Either SEO suffers (all CSR) or servers do pointless work (all SSR).
  • Caching personalised pages. Never ISR/CDN-cache a page that contains user-specific data.
  • Stale critical data. Stock and price at checkout must be checked live, even if the product page is cached.

See it yourself

Open a big e-commerce site and compare View Source across the home page, a product page and the cart: you'll see which ones arrive with content and which are built in the browser.

Quick quiz

What three questions decide a page's rendering strategy?

Does it need SEO? Is it the same for every user? How often does its data change?

Why CSR for checkout?

It's private (no SEO), highly interactive, personalised, and users are already engaged, so first-paint speed matters less than interactivity.

How can a cached product page still show live stock?

Render the static content with ISR/SSG and fetch stock in a small client component (or stream it) on each visit.

title: Finale
text: Blog = SSG (+ ISR, islands). Amazon = SSR (fast paint, then JS makes it interactive). Gmail = CSR + client routing (slow start, instant after). Modern toolbox (streaming, RSC, actions, edge, resumability) = less work on the user's phone without losing interactivity.
html:
• Blog = SSG (+ ISR, islands). Amazon = SSR (fast paint, then JS makes it interactive). Gmail = CSR + client routing (slow start, instant after).
  • Modern toolbox (streaming, RSC, actions, edge, resumability) = less work on the user's phone without losing interactivity.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Blog → SSG (plus ISR and islands): fast, cheap, mostly static.
  • Amazon-style store → SSR / ISR: content visible fast for users and search engines, then JS makes it interactive.
  • Gmail-style app → CSR + client routing: slow first load, instant afterwards.
  • Modern tools (streaming, server components, server actions, edge, resumability) all aim at the same goal: less work on the user's phone without losing interactivity.

Interview answer

There's no single best rendering strategy. Content sites like blogs fit static generation with incremental regeneration and a few interactive islands. Commerce and media sites benefit from server rendering or ISR for fast first paint and SEO, followed by hydration. Long-lived apps like email clients accept a slower first load for an app-like experience with client-side rendering and routing. Newer techniques such as streaming SSR, server components and resumability exist to reduce how much JavaScript the user's device must download and execute.

The analogy

Choosing transport: walking for 500 metres (SSG), an auto for a few kilometres (SSR), and a car you own for daily long commutes (CSR). The right choice depends on the trip, not on which vehicle is "best".

How it works

Common traps

  • Choosing by trend. Pick by page needs: SEO, personalisation, freshness, interactivity.
  • Ignoring the device. Most users are on mid-range phones; JS cost matters more than server speed.
  • Forgetting caching. Many "SSR is slow" problems are really "nothing is cached".

See it yourself

Pick three sites you use daily (a blog, a shop, an email app). Compare View Source and DevTools Performance filmstrips with CPU throttling, and guess the strategy each uses.

Quick quiz

Why does Gmail accept a slow first load?

Users stay for long sessions, and after the first load every action is instant because only data is fetched. SEO doesn't matter for a private inbox.

What's the common goal of streaming, RSC and resumability?

Reduce the work and JavaScript the user's device has to do, while keeping the page fast to show and interactive.

Name the strategy: same for everyone, changes daily, needs SEO.

ISR (or SSG with frequent rebuilds).

title: 100 ms = money
text: Google research: 53% of mobile visits are abandoned if a page takes > 3 s. Often-quoted Amazon finding: +100 ms ≈ −1% sales. Response-time limits (Nielsen): 0.1 s feels instant · 1 s keeps flow · 10 s loses attention. deep_html:
Key points

  • Speed is money: Google's research found 53% of mobile visits are abandoned when a page takes over 3 seconds. An often-quoted Amazon test found +100 ms ≈ −1% sales.
  • Human time limits: 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps you in flow, 10 s and attention is gone.
  • Performance has two jobs: be fast (send less, do less) and feel fast (show useful content early, respond instantly).

Interview answer

Performance directly affects business metrics like conversion and bounce rate, especially on mobile networks. I think of it as two goals: actually being fast, by sending fewer bytes and doing less work on the main thread, and feeling fast, by showing meaningful content early and giving immediate feedback on interactions. I measure with real-user data at the 75th percentile rather than averages, because averages hide the slow users who are most likely to leave.

The analogy

A queue at a bank. Even if total service time is the same, a counter that greets you instantly and hands you a token feels faster than one where you stand in silence. Real speed and perceived speed both matter.

How it works

  • Be fast: smaller bundles, compressed images, fewer requests, caching, less main-thread work.
  • Feel fast: skeletons instead of spinners, render above-the-fold first, instant button feedback, optimistic UI.

Common traps

  • Using averages. An average of 1.5 s can hide 25% of users waiting 5 s. Report the 75th percentile (p75).
  • Testing on a fast laptop and fibre. Most users are on mid-range Android phones and mobile data.
  • Spinners for everything. A skeleton that matches the final layout feels faster than a blank spinner.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → throttling Slow 4G (and Performance → CPU 4x slowdown) → reload your site. That's closer to what many users see.

Quick quiz

Why report p75 instead of the average?

Averages hide the slow tail. p75 means 75% of visits were at least this fast, so it captures the experience of slower users too.

What's the difference between being fast and feeling fast?

Being fast reduces actual load and processing time. Feeling fast changes what users see and when (early content, instant feedback), so waiting is less noticeable.

What are the 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s limits?

0.1 s feels instantaneous, 1 s keeps the user's flow of thought, 10 s is the limit of attention.

title: Core Web Vitals
text: LCP (loading) ≤ 2.5 s · INP (responsiveness) ≤ 200 ms · CLS (visual stability) ≤ 0.1. Graded at the 75th percentile of real Chrome visits (CrUX), mobile and desktop separately. See it: PageSpeed Insights → "Discover what your real users are experiencing". Trap: INP replaced FID in March 2024.

deep_html:
Key points

  • Google's Core Web Vitals are three metrics for real user experience:
  • LCP (loading) ≤ 2.5 s · INP (responsiveness) ≤ 200 ms · CLS (visual stability) ≤ 0.1.
  • They're graded at the 75th percentile of real Chrome visits (CrUX data), separately for mobile and desktop. INP replaced FID in March 2024.

Interview answer

Core Web Vitals are Google's user-centric metrics. Largest Contentful Paint measures loading, with good at 2.5 seconds or less. Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness to clicks, taps and key presses, with good at 200 ms or less. Cumulative Layout Shift measures unexpected movement, with good at 0.1 or less. They're assessed at the 75th percentile of real user visits from the Chrome UX Report, mobile and desktop separately, and they're a factor in Google Search ranking.

The analogy

A restaurant review with three scores: how fast your food arrived (LCP), how quickly the waiter responds when you call (INP), and whether the table wobbles and spills your drink (CLS).

How it works

  • A page "passes" when all three are good at p75.
  • Data comes from real Chrome users over a rolling 28-day window (CrUX), so fixes take weeks to show fully.

Common traps

  • FID is gone. INP replaced it in March 2024 and is much harder to pass.
  • Lab ≠ field. Lighthouse can't measure INP (no real interactions); use field data to judge.
  • Mobile and desktop are separate. Passing on desktop says little about mobile.

See it yourself

PageSpeed Insights → enter any URL → the top section "Discover what your real users are experiencing" shows field LCP, INP and CLS at p75.

Quick quiz

Name the three Core Web Vitals and their "good" thresholds.

LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1.

Which percentile is used to assess a page?

The 75th percentile of page visits.

What metric did INP replace?

First Input Delay (FID), in March 2024.

title: LCP
text: Time until the largest image / text block in the viewport renders. Candidates: , video poster, CSS background image, text blocks. 4 parts: TTFB → resource load delay → load duration → render delay. Usually the delay (image found late) is the problem. See it: Performance panel → LCP marker + LCP breakdown insight. Trap: loading="lazy" on the hero makes LCP worse.

• Time until the largest image / text block in the viewport renders. Candidates: <img>, video poster, CSS background image, text blocks.
  • 4 parts: TTFB → resource load delay → load duration → render delay. Usually the delay (image found late) is the problem.
  • See it: Performance panel → LCP marker + LCP breakdown insight. Trap: loading="lazy" on the hero makes LCP worse.
deep_html:
Key points

  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) = time until the largest image or text block in the viewport is painted. Good ≤ 2.5 s.
  • Candidates: <img>, a video's poster, a CSS background image, a big block of text.
  • LCP splits into 4 parts: TTFB → load delay → load duration → render delay. The usual culprit is load delay: the image is discovered late.

Interview answer

LCP measures when the largest visible content element finishes rendering. I break it into time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay. Most slow LCPs come from the hero image being discovered late, for example because it's set in CSS, injected by JavaScript or lazy-loaded. Fixes are putting the image directly in the HTML, adding fetchpriority high or a preload, serving a properly sized modern format from a CDN, and keeping render-blocking resources small.

The analogy

A stage show where the main actor arrives late. The stage, lights and curtains were ready early, but the audience feels the show started only when the star walked on.

How it works

<!-- Discoverable early, high priority, NOT lazy -->
<img src="/hero-1200.avif" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high" alt="New collection">

Common traps

  • loading="lazy" on the hero image delays it until layout. Never lazy-load above-the-fold images.
  • Hero as a CSS background or rendered by client JS: the preload scanner can't see it early.
  • Huge images. A 3000 px JPEG on a phone wastes seconds; serve responsive sizes in AVIF/WebP.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record a page load → the LCP marker shows which element it was; the LCP breakdown insight shows the 4 sub-parts.

Quick quiz

What elements can be the LCP element?

Images (including SVG images inside, video posters, CSS background images) and block-level text elements in the viewport.

The hero image downloads in 200 ms but LCP is 4 s. Where do you look?

TTFB, load delay (the image was found late) and render delay (render-blocking CSS/JS).

Why does lazy-loading the hero hurt LCP?

Lazy images wait until layout confirms they're near the viewport, so the download starts much later.

title: CLS
text: Sum of unexpected shifts; each = impact × distance; grouped into bursts (session windows); your worst burst = CLS. Culprits: images without width/height, ads/embeds without reserved space, injected banners, font swaps. Fix: reserve space ( width/height , aspect-ratio , min-height ). See it: Rendering → Layout Shift Regions. Trap: shifts within 500 ms of a tap/keypress are excluded; transform animations never shift layout.
html:
• Sum of unexpected shifts; each = impact × distance; grouped into bursts (session windows); your worst burst = CLS.
  • Culprits: images without width/height, ads/embeds without reserved space, injected banners, font swaps. Fix: reserve space (width/height, aspect-ratio, min-height).
  • See it: Rendering → Layout Shift Regions. Trap: shifts within 500 ms of a tap/keypress are excluded; transform animations never shift layout.
deep_html:
Key points

  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much visible content moves unexpectedly while someone uses the page.
  • Good ≤ 0.1, poor > 0.25. It's one of Google's three Core Web Vitals, with LCP (loading) and INP (responsiveness).
  • Almost every shift has the same fix: reserve the space before the content arrives.

Interview answer

CLS measures how much visible content moves unexpectedly. Each shift scores impact fraction times distance fraction, shifts are grouped into bursts, and the worst burst is the CLS. Good is 0.1 or less. The main causes are images without dimensions, ads and embeds without reserved space, injected banners and font swaps, and the fix is always to reserve space before the content arrives.

The analogy

Someone pulls your chair away just as you sit down. The chair was fine; it just moved at the worst moment. That's a layout shift: you aim for "Cancel", an ad loads above it, everything slides down, and your thumb lands on "Buy".

How it actually works

Each time a visible element moves without the user causing it, the browser records a layout shift and gives it a score:

shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction

  • Impact fraction: how much of the viewport the moving elements touched (before + after positions combined).
  • Distance fraction: how far they moved, as a fraction of the viewport's height (or width).

Example: an article covers 50% of the screen. A banner loads above it and pushes it down by 25% of the screen height. The article now touches 75% of the viewport (old + new area), so impact = 0.75, distance = 0.25 → score 0.19. One banner, and you're already in "needs improvement".

Bursts, not totals

Shifts that happen close together are grouped into a session window (gaps under 1 second, the window capped at 5 seconds). Your page's CLS is the score of its worst window, so one bad moment decides the number, no matter how long the user stays.

The usual culprits and their fixes

1. Images and videos without dimensions. The browser doesn't know how tall they'll be until they load.

<!-- The browser computes the aspect ratio from these and reserves the box -->
<img src="hero.jpg" width="1200" height="675" alt="…">

img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }   /* stays responsive, keeps the ratio */
.video-embed { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%; }

2. Ads, embeds and iframes. Reserve the slot's most likely size:

.ad-slot { min-height: 250px; }   /* don't collapse it to 0 when there's no ad */

3. Content injected above what the user is reading (cookie banners, "download our app" bars, late-loading announcements). Put them in reserved space, overlay them (position: fixed), or insert them below the fold.

4. Web fonts swapping in. A fallback font with different letter widths reflows the text when the real font arrives. Preload the key font and match the fallback's size:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

@font-face {
  font-family: 'Inter Fallback';
  src: local('Arial');
  size-adjust: 107%;   /* tune so Arial takes the same space as Inter */
}
body { font-family: 'Inter', 'Inter Fallback', sans-serif; }

5. Animating layout properties. Animating top, height or margin moves other elements. Animate transform instead: it moves pixels without changing layout, so it never counts as a shift.

Measure it in code

let cls = 0;
new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (!entry.hadRecentInput) {   // shifts right after a tap/keypress don't count
      cls += entry.value;
      console.log('shift', entry.value.toFixed(3), entry.sources?.map(s => s.node));
    }
  }
}).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });

(This simple sum ignores session windows; for the real number use Google's web-vitals library: onCLS(console.log).)

See it yourself

  • DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Rendering → tick Layout Shift Regions. Every shift flashes blue.
  • DevTools → Performance → record a page load → the Layout shifts track shows each one and which element moved.
  • Lighthouse / PageSpeed Insights → "Avoid large layout shifts" lists the guilty elements.

Real-world story

Yahoo! JAPAN News (over 22 billion page views a month) fixed late-loading images that shoved text down by reserving their space. Its layout-shift score dropped from about 0.2 to almost zero, and readers viewed about 15% more pages per session with 13% longer sessions. (Reel: The page that jumps under your thumb.)

Common mistakes

  • Testing only on a fast laptop. Shifts happen when things load late: test with Network throttling on "Slow 4G".
  • Setting height in CSS but width: 100%. The image stretches. Use width/height attributes plus height: auto, or aspect-ratio.
  • Collapsing empty ad slots. If no ad fills, keep the reserved space (or a placeholder), or the content jumps up.

Interview questions

What is CLS and what counts as a good score?

The largest burst of unexpected layout shifts during the page's life. Each shift = impact fraction × distance fraction. Good ≤ 0.1, needs improvement up to 0.25, poor above 0.25.

Does every movement count as a layout shift?

No. Shifts within 500 ms of a user input (tap, click, keypress) are expected and excluded. Movement done with CSS transform doesn't change layout, so it never counts. Content appearing at the end of the page without moving anything doesn't count either.

How do you prevent layout shift from images?

Always give width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) so the browser reserves the box before the image downloads; keep it responsive with max-width: 100%; height: auto.

A cookie banner is causing CLS. What are your options?

Make it an overlay (position: fixed), reserve its space from the first paint (render it server-side), or place it at the bottom where it doesn't push content.

title: INP
text: Input → next paint. Parts: input delay (main thread busy) + processing (handlers) + presentation delay (style/layout/paint). Roughly your worst interaction of the visit, not an average. Fix: feedback first, await scheduler.yield() , heavy work after; break long tasks. See it: Performance panel live metrics → interactions list. Trap: scroll and hover are not counted — only click, tap, key press.
html:
• Input → next paint. Parts: input delay (main thread busy) + processing (handlers) + presentation delay (style/layout/paint).
  • Roughly your worst interaction of the visit, not an average. Fix: feedback first, await scheduler.yield(), heavy work after; break long tasks.
  • See it: Performance panel live metrics → interactions list. Trap: scroll and hover are not counted — only click, tap, key press.
deep_html:
Key points

  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint) = time from a click, tap or key press to the next frame painted on screen. Good ≤ 200 ms.
  • It has three parts: input delay (main thread busy) + processing (your handlers) + presentation delay (style, layout, paint).
  • It reflects roughly your worst interaction during the visit, not the average.

Interview answer

INP measures responsiveness across all clicks, taps and key presses during a page visit, and reports roughly the slowest one. Each interaction is input delay while the main thread is busy, then the event handlers' processing time, then the presentation delay until the next frame paints. To improve it I show visual feedback first and defer heavy work by yielding, for example with scheduler.yield, I break up long tasks, reduce rendering work, and move heavy computation off the main thread.

The analogy

Pressing a lift button. INP isn't about how fast the lift arrives; it's about how fast the button lights up to say "got it". A button that lights up instantly feels responsive even if the lift takes a while.

How it works

button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  button.classList.add('loading');                 // 1. instant feedback
  await (globalThis.scheduler?.yield?.() ?? new Promise(r => setTimeout(r)));   // 2. let it paint
  runExpensiveFilter();                            // 3. heavy work after
});

Common traps

  • Scrolling and hovering don't count. Only clicks, taps and keyboard input.
  • Lighthouse can't measure INP (it doesn't interact). Use field data or record interactions yourself.
  • Huge re-renders in React on a click are a classic INP problem: smaller components, transitions, virtualisation.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance panel → live metrics view shows INP as you click around, with a list of interactions and their timing breakdown.

Quick quiz

What are the three phases of an interaction?

Input delay, processing time, presentation delay.

Does scrolling affect INP?

No. Only clicks, taps and key presses are measured.

How can you improve INP without making the work faster?

Show feedback immediately, then yield to the browser so it paints before running the heavy work.

title: TTFB · FCP · TBT
text: TTFB (first byte, good ≤ 0.8 s) → FCP (first anything, ≤ 1.8 s) → LCP. Slow TTFB = server, distance, redirects → CDN, caching. TBT = sum over long tasks of (duration − 50 ms) between FCP and interactive. Lab stand-in for INP; Lighthouse weight 30% (largest). Puzzle: tasks 70, 140, 40 ms → TBT = 20 + 90 + 0 = 110 ms .
html:
• TTFB (first byte, good ≤ 0.8 s) → FCP (first anything, ≤ 1.8 s) → LCP. Slow TTFB = server, distance, redirects → CDN, caching.
  • TBT = sum over long tasks of (duration − 50 ms) between FCP and interactive. Lab stand-in for INP; Lighthouse weight 30% (largest).
  • Puzzle: tasks 70, 140, 40 ms → TBT = 20 + 90 + 0 = 110 ms.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Load timeline: TTFB (first byte, good ≤ 0.8 s) → FCP (first content painted, good ≤ 1.8 s) → LCP.
  • Slow TTFB = server time, distance, redirects. Fix with CDNs, caching and fewer redirects.
  • TBT (Total Blocking Time) = for each long task between FCP and interactive, add (duration − 50 ms). It's Lighthouse's lab stand-in for INP and its biggest-weighted metric.

Interview answer

TTFB measures time until the first byte of the HTML arrives, which reflects server processing, network distance and redirects. FCP is when the first text or image is painted. LCP is when the largest element is painted. TBT is a lab metric: for every long task between FCP and Time to Interactive, it sums the time beyond 50 ms. It correlates with responsiveness and carries the largest weight in the Lighthouse performance score, at 30%.

The analogy

Waiting for a train. TTFB: the train appears on the horizon. FCP: the first carriage reaches the platform. LCP: the carriage you're boarding arrives. TBT: how long the doors stayed jammed shut after that.

How it works

TBT puzzle: three tasks of 70 ms, 140 ms and 40 ms → (70−50) + (140−50) + 0 = 110 ms. The 40 ms task isn't long, so it adds nothing.

Common traps

  • Redirect chains. http → https → www → /en adds a full round trip per hop before TTFB.
  • TBT is lab-only. It's a proxy; real responsiveness is INP in the field.
  • Fast TTFB but slow FCP usually means render-blocking CSS or JS.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → document request → Timing for TTFB ("Waiting for server response"). Lighthouse → Performance → metrics section for FCP, LCP and TBT.

Quick quiz

Calculate TBT for tasks of 120 ms, 50 ms and 80 ms.

70 + 0 + 30 = 100 ms. A 50 ms task isn't over the threshold.

What usually causes a slow TTFB?

Slow server processing or database queries, a server far from the user, no caching, and redirect chains.

Which Lighthouse metric has the highest weight?

Total Blocking Time (30%).

title: Lab vs field
text: Lab (Lighthouse): one run, simulated mid-range phone, throttled, clean browser → repeatable, for debugging. Field (CrUX / RUM): real users, 28 days, p75. They disagree: lab has no INP, only first screen, one device. RUM: import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals' + navigator.sendBeacon . Trap: CrUX is a 28-day rolling window → fixes fade in over weeks.
html:
• Lab (Lighthouse): one run, simulated mid-range phone, throttled, clean browser → repeatable, for debugging.
  • Field (CrUX / RUM): real users, 28 days, p75. They disagree: lab has no INP, only first screen, one device.
  • RUM: import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals' + navigator.sendBeacon. Trap: CrUX is a 28-day rolling window → fixes fade in over weeks.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Lab data (Lighthouse): one run, simulated mid-range phone, throttled network, clean browser. Repeatable, good for debugging.
  • Field data (CrUX, RUM): real users on real devices, over 28 days, at p75. This is what users and Google actually judge you on.
  • They often disagree, and field data wins.

Interview answer

Lab tools like Lighthouse run a controlled test on a simulated device, which makes them repeatable and great for diagnosing issues, but they only cover the initial load, one device profile and no real interactions, so there's no INP. Field data comes from real users, through the Chrome UX Report or my own real user monitoring with the web-vitals library, aggregated at the 75th percentile. I use field data to decide what's wrong and lab tools to debug and verify fixes.

The analogy

A car's fuel economy on the official test track versus what you actually get in Bangalore traffic. The test is useful for comparing cars; your real mileage is what matters to your wallet.

How it works

// Your own real-user monitoring
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals';
const send = m => navigator.sendBeacon('/analytics', JSON.stringify(m));
onLCP(send); onINP(send); onCLS(send);

Common traps

  • "Lighthouse 98, but Search Console says poor." Real users have slower devices and interact with the page; lab can't see that.
  • Expecting fixes to show instantly. CrUX is a 28-day window, so improvements fade in over weeks.
  • Low-traffic pages may have no CrUX data; your own RUM fills the gap.

See it yourself

PageSpeed Insights shows both: the top section is field (real users), the bottom is lab (Lighthouse). Compare them for the same URL.

Quick quiz

Why can't Lighthouse measure INP?

It loads the page without interacting with it, so there are no clicks or taps to measure. It reports TBT as a proxy.

What's CrUX?

The Chrome UX Report: field performance data from opted-in Chrome users, aggregated per origin/URL over 28 days.

When do you use lab tools if field data is what counts?

To debug, reproduce and verify fixes quickly in a controlled environment before field data catches up.

title: IQ: measuring performance
text: CWV + thresholds at p75 · Lighthouse 98 but poor INP (no interactions, TBT is a proxy, real devices, 28 days) · slow LCP with fast image download (TTFB, load delay → in HTML + preload/fetchpriority, render delay) · banner CLS (reserve, overlay, transform).
