deep_html:
Key points

  • This is a revision episode: four interview questions on measuring performance.
  • Know the Core Web Vitals thresholds, why lab and field disagree, how to debug a slow LCP, and how to fix a banner causing CLS.

Interview answer

I measure with field data first: Core Web Vitals at the 75th percentile, LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1. Lab tools help me find causes. For each problem I break the metric into parts, like LCP's TTFB, load delay, load time and render delay, and fix the biggest part rather than guessing.

Quick quiz

What are the Core Web Vitals, their thresholds, and at what percentile?

LCP ≤ 2.5 s (loading), INP ≤ 200 ms (responsiveness), CLS ≤ 0.1 (visual stability), all assessed at the 75th percentile of real visits, mobile and desktop separately.

Lighthouse gives 98, but field INP is poor. Why?

Lighthouse doesn't interact with the page, so it can't measure INP (TBT is only a proxy). It uses one simulated device, while real users run slower phones, have extensions, use the page for minutes and click things. Field data is also a 28-day window, so it may reflect older code.

The hero image downloads fast, but LCP is still slow. How do you debug it?

Break LCP into parts. Slow TTFB → server/CDN/caching. Big load delay → the image is discovered late: put it in the HTML as an <img>, add fetchpriority="high" or a preload, remove lazy loading. Big render delay → render-blocking CSS/JS or client-side rendering is holding the paint.

A cookie banner causes CLS. What are your options?

Reserve its space from the first paint, render it as an overlay with position: fixed so it doesn't push content, or animate it in with transform, which doesn't shift layout.

title: Critical rendering path
text: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → first pixels. CSS is render-blocking ; plain <script> is parser-blocking . Shrink it: inline critical CSS, load the rest non-blocking, media="print" for non-critical sheets, defer scripts. See it: Lighthouse "Render blocking requests"; Performance panel request details "Render blocking". Trap: a script after a stylesheet waits for that CSS → CSS can block parsing too.
html:
• HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → first pixels. CSS is render-blocking; plain <script> is parser-blocking.
  • Shrink it: inline critical CSS, load the rest non-blocking, media="print" for non-critical sheets, defer scripts.
  • See it: Lighthouse "Render blocking requests"; Performance panel request details "Render blocking". Trap: a script after a stylesheet waits for that CSS → CSS can block parsing too.
deep_html:
Key points

  • The critical rendering path is everything the browser needs before the first pixels: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → paint.
  • CSS is render-blocking (no paint until it's loaded). A plain <script> is parser-blocking (HTML parsing stops until it runs).
  • Shrink the path: inline critical CSS, load the rest without blocking, and defer scripts.

Interview answer

The critical rendering path is the sequence from receiving HTML to the first paint: building the DOM, building the CSSOM, combining them into the render tree, then layout and paint. Stylesheets block rendering and synchronous scripts block parsing, and a script also waits for any stylesheet before it. To speed up first paint I inline the small amount of CSS needed above the fold, load the remaining CSS asynchronously or with media queries, and defer scripts so they don't block parsing.

The analogy

Opening a shop in the morning. You can't open the shutters until the essentials are on the shelves (critical CSS). The stockroom can be organised after customers walk in.

How it works

<head>
  <style>/* critical above-the-fold CSS, inlined */</style>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">         <!-- doesn't block screen rendering -->
  <link rel="preload" href="/rest.css" as="style" onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">
  <script src="/app.js" defer></script>
</head>

Common traps

  • A script after a stylesheet waits for that CSS, because scripts may read styles. So CSS can indirectly block parsing too.
  • Huge inlined CSS makes the HTML heavier and isn't cached. Inline only what's needed above the fold.
  • @import inside CSS creates a chain: one file must download before the next is discovered.

See it yourself

Lighthouse → "Eliminate render-blocking resources" lists the CSS/JS delaying first paint. In the Performance panel, request details show Render blocking: Blocking.

Quick quiz

Why is CSS render-blocking but not parser-blocking?

The browser can keep building the DOM, but it won't paint without styles to avoid a flash of unstyled content.

How can CSS end up blocking parsing?

A synchronous script that follows a stylesheet waits for that stylesheet to load, and the parser waits for the script.

Name two ways to load non-critical CSS without blocking render.

Use a media attribute that doesn't match (e.g. media="print", then switch), or preload it and swap rel to stylesheet on load.

title: async vs defer
text: plain: stop parsing, fetch, run. async : fetch in parallel, run on arrival, no order. defer : fetch in parallel, run after parsing, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded. defer → app code; async → independent scripts (analytics). type="module" is deferred by default. Trap: async scripts that depend on each other break randomly; defer does nothing on inline scripts.
html:
• plain: stop parsing, fetch, run. async: fetch in parallel, run on arrival, no order. defer: fetch in parallel, run after parsing, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded.
  • defer → app code; async → independent scripts (analytics). type="module" is deferred by default.
  • Trap: async scripts that depend on each other break randomly; defer does nothing on inline scripts.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Plain <script>: stop parsing, download, run, then continue.
  • async: download in parallel, run as soon as it arrives, in any order.
  • defer: download in parallel, run after parsing finishes, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded. type="module" scripts are deferred by default.

Interview answer

A classic script blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and executes. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it's ready, which can be before or after parsing and in any order, so it suits independent scripts like analytics. defer also downloads in parallel but waits until the document is parsed and runs scripts in order, so it's the right default for application code that depends on the DOM or on other scripts. Module scripts behave like defer by default.

The analogy

Guests arriving at a wedding. Plain: the ceremony stops every time a guest walks in. async: guests walk in whenever they arrive and start dancing immediately, in random order. defer: guests wait outside and walk in together, in the order on the list, after the ceremony.

How it works

<script src="/vendor.js" defer></script>
<script src="/app.js" defer></script>            <!-- runs after vendor.js -->
<script src="https://analytics.example.com/a.js" async></script>

Common traps

  • Dependent scripts with async break randomly, because the order changes with network timing.
  • defer does nothing on inline scripts. It only applies to scripts with src.
  • async doesn't make the script cheap. It still runs on the main thread when it arrives.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record a load: plain scripts appear as gaps in HTML parsing; deferred scripts run as a group after parsing.

Quick quiz

Which attribute keeps execution order?

defer (and module scripts by default). async does not.

Where would you use async?

For independent third-party scripts like analytics that don't depend on other scripts or on the DOM being complete.

When do deferred scripts run relative to DOMContentLoaded?

After parsing completes and before the DOMContentLoaded event fires.

title: Resource hints
text: preconnect (DNS+TCP+TLS early) · dns-prefetch (DNS only) · preload (this page, late-discovered, high priority, needs as ) · prefetch (next page, lowest priority). See it: Network → Priority column. Trap: preloading everything steals bandwidth; Chrome warns about unused preloads; font preload needs crossorigin or it downloads twice.
html:
• preconnect (DNS+TCP+TLS early) · dns-prefetch (DNS only) · preload (this page, late-discovered, high priority, needs as) · prefetch (next page, lowest priority).
  • See it: Network → Priority column. Trap: preloading everything steals bandwidth; Chrome warns about unused preloads; font preload needs crossorigin or it downloads twice.
deep_html:
Key points

  • preconnect: do DNS + TCP + TLS to another origin early. dns-prefetch: DNS only (cheaper).
  • preload: download a resource this page needs, found late, at high priority. Needs as.
  • prefetch: download something for the next page, at lowest priority.

Interview answer

Resource hints let me tell the browser about work before it would discover it. preconnect sets up the connection to a critical third-party origin, like a font or image CDN. dns-prefetch does only the DNS lookup and is a cheaper fallback. preload fetches a resource the current page definitely needs but discovers late, such as the hero image or a font, with the right as attribute. prefetch downloads resources for a likely next navigation at idle priority. Overusing preload hurts because it competes for bandwidth.

The analogy

Planning a trip. preconnect = book the cab in advance. preload = pack the passport first because you definitely need it today. prefetch = keep tomorrow's clothes ready in case you go out.

How it works

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://images.example-cdn.com">
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/hero.avif" as="image" fetchpriority="high">
<link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout.js">

Common traps

  • Preloading everything steals bandwidth from what matters; Chrome warns about preloads not used within a few seconds.
  • Font preload without crossorigin downloads the font twice (fonts are fetched in CORS mode).
  • Too many preconnects waste sockets and CPU on connections you may not use.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → right-click headers → enable Priority. Add a preload and watch the resource move earlier with High priority.

Quick quiz

preload vs prefetch?

preload is for the current page, high priority, things needed soon. prefetch is for a future navigation, lowest priority.

Why must font preloads include crossorigin?

Fonts are requested in CORS mode; without crossorigin the preload doesn't match the real request, so the font downloads twice.

What does preconnect save?

The DNS lookup, TCP handshake and TLS handshake to that origin, done before the first request needs them.

title: Code splitting
text: Dynamic import() → separate chunk loaded on demand. Split by route, heavy feature, below the fold; shared libs in a vendor chunk. See it: DevTools → Coverage (red = downloaded, never ran). Trap: too many tiny chunks → request waterfalls.
html:
• Dynamic import() → separate chunk loaded on demand. Split by route, heavy feature, below the fold; shared libs in a vendor chunk.
  • See it: DevTools → Coverage (red = downloaded, never ran). Trap: too many tiny chunks → request waterfalls.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Code splitting breaks one big bundle into smaller chunks that load only when needed, using dynamic import().
  • Split by route, by heavy feature (charts, editors, maps), and by below-the-fold components. Shared libraries go in a vendor chunk.
  • Goal: the first page downloads and runs only its own code.

Interview answer

Code splitting uses dynamic imports so the bundler emits separate chunks that are loaded on demand. I usually split by route first, then lazy-load heavy, rarely used features like rich text editors, charts or maps, and keep shared dependencies in a common chunk so they're cached across routes. The DevTools Coverage tab shows how much downloaded code never runs, which is a good signal for what to split. I avoid splitting too finely, because many tiny chunks create request waterfalls.

The analogy

A travel guidebook split into city booklets. You carry only the city you're visiting today instead of the whole 800-page book.

How it works

// Load the chart library only when the user opens the report
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const { renderChart } = await import('./chart.js');   // separate chunk
  renderChart(data);
});

Common traps

  • Too many tiny chunks → request waterfalls (chunk A loads, then discovers it needs chunk B).
  • Splitting what's always needed just adds a delay.
  • No loading state. Lazy chunks take time; show a fallback.

See it yourself

DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Coverage → reload. Red bars are code that was downloaded but never executed, your splitting opportunities.

Quick quiz

What creates a split point in modern bundlers?

A dynamic import() expression.

What should you split first?

Routes, then large features used by few users or only after interaction.

What's the risk of over-splitting?

Many small requests and dependency waterfalls that can make loading slower.

title: Lazy routes
text: const Orders = lazy(() => import('./pages/Orders')) inside <Suspense fallback> . Hide the delay: prefetch on hover / in viewport (Next.js <Link> does this in production). Rules: never lazy-load the landing route; fallbacks must hold layout. Trap: after a deploy, old tabs hit ChunkLoadError → keep old chunks, catch + reload.
html:
• const Orders = lazy(() => import('./pages/Orders')) inside <Suspense fallback>. Hide the delay: prefetch on hover / in viewport (Next.js <Link> does this in production).
  • Rules: never lazy-load the landing route; fallbacks must hold layout. Trap: after a deploy, old tabs hit ChunkLoadError → keep old chunks, catch + reload.
deep_html:
Key points

  • In React, lazy routes use React.lazy(() => import('./Page')) wrapped in <Suspense fallback>.
  • Hide the delay by prefetching the route's chunk on hover or when the link is visible (Next.js <Link> does this in production).
  • After a deploy, old tabs may request chunks that no longer exist: handle ChunkLoadError.

Interview answer

I lazy-load routes with React.lazy and a dynamic import, wrapped in a Suspense boundary with a fallback that holds the layout. To avoid a visible delay on navigation, I prefetch chunks when a link is hovered or enters the viewport. I never lazy-load the landing route itself. In production I keep old chunk files available for a while after deploys and catch chunk load failures to reload the page, because users with an old tab open will request files from the previous build.

The analogy

A restaurant that starts cooking your dessert when you glance at the dessert menu, so it's ready the moment you order it.

How it works

const Orders = lazy(() => import('./pages/Orders'));
const prefetchOrders = () => import('./pages/Orders');

<Link to="/orders" onMouseEnter={prefetchOrders}>Orders</Link>

<Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
  <Routes><Route path="/orders" element={<Orders />} /></Routes>
</Suspense>

Common traps

  • Lazy-loading the landing route delays the first paint for everyone.
  • Fallbacks that don't hold layout cause layout shift when the page arrives.
  • ChunkLoadError after deploys. Keep old chunks for a while, and on failure reload once.

See it yourself

In a React app with lazy routes, DevTools → Network → JS filter → navigate: a new chunk loads per route. Hover a prefetched link and watch it load before the click.

Quick quiz

Which component must wrap a lazy component?

<Suspense> with a fallback.

How do you make lazy routes feel instant?

Prefetch the chunk on hover, focus or when the link enters the viewport.

Why do users get ChunkLoadError after a deploy?

Their open tab still references the old build's chunk filenames, which were removed by the new deploy.

title: Tree shaking
text: Bundler follows imports from the entry, keeps used exports, drops the rest. Needs ES modules (static); CommonJS require usually can't be shaken. Side effects: mark "sideEffects": false (or a list) in package.json. import _ from 'lodash' ≈ 70 KB vs import { debounce } from 'lodash-es' . Trap: barrel files ( export * from … ) can pull whole libraries in → import from the file directly.
html:
• Bundler follows imports from the entry, keeps used exports, drops the rest. Needs ES modules (static); CommonJS require usually can't be shaken.
  • Side effects: mark "sideEffects": false (or a list) in package.json. import _ from 'lodash' ≈ 70 KB vs import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'.
  • Trap: barrel files (export * from …) can pull whole libraries in → import from the file directly.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Tree shaking: the bundler follows imports from your entry file, keeps exports that are used, and drops the rest.
  • It needs ES modules (import/export), which are static. CommonJS require() usually can't be shaken.
  • import _ from 'lodash' pulls in about 70 KB; import { debounce } from 'lodash-es' pulls in only what you use.

Interview answer

Tree shaking is dead-code elimination based on the static structure of ES module imports and exports. The bundler marks which exports are actually used and removes the unused ones during minification. It fails with CommonJS modules, with code that has side effects the bundler must keep, with dynamic property access, and with barrel files that re-export everything. Marking packages as side-effect-free in package.json and importing specific functions helps it work.

The analogy

Packing for a trip by following a checklist of what you'll actually wear. Anything not on the list stays in the cupboard. But if an item is glued to something you need (side effects), it comes along too.

How it works

// package.json of your library
{ "sideEffects": false }
// or list files that DO have side effects:
{ "sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"] }

Common traps

  • Barrel files (index.js with export * from …) can make the bundler keep far more than you use.
  • CSS imports are side effects. Marking everything side-effect-free can drop your CSS.
  • Only works in production builds with minification on; dev bundles keep everything.

See it yourself

Build your app and open a bundle analyzer (e.g. vite-bundle-visualizer or webpack-bundle-analyzer). Look for whole libraries where you only use one function.

Quick quiz

Why does tree shaking need ES modules?

ES imports/exports are static, so the bundler can know what's used at build time. require() is dynamic and evaluated at runtime.

What does "sideEffects": false tell the bundler?

That importing a module has no effect besides its exports, so unused modules can be dropped completely.

Give two reasons unused code might stay in the bundle.

CommonJS modules, side effects, barrel re-exports, or dynamic property access on a namespace import.

title: Bundle diet
text: 100 KB of JS ≠ 100 KB of image: JS is downloaded, parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread. Measure (bundle analyzer), then: moment → date-fns / Intl, drop unneeded polyfills, dedupe versions, check bundlephobia, use the platform (fetch, <dialog> ). Trap: "200 KB gzipped" — the browser parses the uncompressed size (~700 KB). Compression saves network, not CPU.
html:
• 100 KB of JS ≠ 100 KB of image: JS is downloaded, parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread.
  • Measure (bundle analyzer), then: moment → date-fns / Intl, drop unneeded polyfills, dedupe versions, check bundlephobia, use the platform (fetch, <dialog>).
  • Trap: "200 KB gzipped" — the browser parses the uncompressed size (~700 KB). Compression saves network, not CPU.
deep_html:
Key points

  • 100 KB of JS costs far more than 100 KB of image: JS must be downloaded, parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread.
  • Measure first (bundle analyzer), then cut: replace heavy libraries, drop unneeded polyfills, dedupe versions, use the platform.
  • "200 KB gzipped" is around 700 KB for the browser to parse. Compression saves network, not CPU.

Interview answer

JavaScript is the most expensive asset because after downloading it has to be parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread, which hurts interactivity on slow devices. I start with a bundle analyzer to find the biggest dependencies, then replace heavy libraries with lighter ones or native APIs, remove unnecessary polyfills, dedupe multiple versions of the same package, and code-split the rest. I check package costs before adding them, for example with bundlephobia.

The analogy

Luggage weight vs assembly time. An image is a sealed box: carry it and you're done. JavaScript is flat-pack furniture: carrying it is only the start, you still have to assemble it before you can use it.

How it works

// Built into every modern browser, zero KB
new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { dateStyle: 'medium' }).format(new Date());
new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }).format(1999);

Common traps

  • Judging by gzipped size. The browser parses the uncompressed size.
  • Two versions of the same library (e.g. React-dependent packages pinning different versions) double the cost. Check npm ls <pkg>.
  • Adding a dependency for one function. Check its cost first.

See it yourself

Run a bundle analyzer on your build. Then DevTools → Performance with CPU 4x slowdown → look at the "Evaluate Script" and "Compile" blocks for your main bundle.

Quick quiz

Why is JS more expensive than an image of the same size?

JS must be parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread after downloading; images are decoded mostly off the main thread.

Does gzip reduce parse time?

No. It reduces transfer size; the browser still parses the full uncompressed code.

First step to shrink a large bundle?

Measure with a bundle analyzer to find the biggest contributors before changing anything.

title: Minify + Brotli
text: Minify: strip whitespace/comments, rename locals. Compress: gzip, Brotli (≈ 15–20% smaller than gzip on text). accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd → content-encoding: br . See it: Network → big request rows show transferred vs real size. Trap: don't compress JPEG/PNG/MP4/WOFF2 — already compressed. Compress text: HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG.
html:
• Minify: strip whitespace/comments, rename locals. Compress: gzip, Brotli (≈ 15–20% smaller than gzip on text).
  • accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd → content-encoding: br. See it: Network → big request rows show transferred vs real size.
  • Trap: don't compress JPEG/PNG/MP4/WOFF2 — already compressed. Compress text: HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Minify: remove whitespace and comments, shorten local variable names. Compress: gzip or Brotli (usually 15–20% smaller than gzip for text).
  • The browser says what it accepts (accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd); the server replies with content-encoding: br.
  • Compress text (HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG). Don't re-compress JPEG, PNG, MP4 or WOFF2: they're already compressed.

Interview answer

Minification shrinks code itself by removing whitespace and comments and mangling local names, while compression encodes the bytes for transfer. Browsers advertise supported encodings in accept-encoding, and servers or CDNs respond with Brotli or gzip, indicated by content-encoding. Brotli typically beats gzip on text assets, and static assets can be pre-compressed at build time at maximum level. Already-compressed formats like images, video and woff2 fonts gain nothing from it.

The analogy

Packing clothes for a trip. Minify = fold them neatly and remove the hangers. Compress = vacuum-seal the bag. You don't vacuum-seal something that's already vacuum-sealed.

How it works

GET /assets/app.js
accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd

200 OK
content-encoding: br
content-type: text/javascript

Common traps

  • Compressing images or fonts again wastes CPU for no gain.
  • Dynamic Brotli at max level is slow per request; pre-compress static files at build time instead.
  • Missing compression on JSON APIs. Large API responses benefit just as much as JS.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → enable Big request rows: each row shows transferred size (compressed) above resource size (real). Check content-encoding in the response headers.

Quick quiz

Minification vs compression?

Minification changes the code to be smaller; compression encodes the bytes for transfer and is undone by the browser.

Which header tells you how a response was compressed?

content-encoding (e.g. br or gzip).

Should you Brotli-compress PNG files?

No. PNG, JPEG, MP4 and WOFF2 are already compressed.

title: IQ: loading + bundles
text: When scripts run (plain/async/defer/module) · preconnect vs preload vs prefetch · why tree shaking keeps code (CJS, side effects, barrels, dynamic access) · cutting a 1.5 MB bundle (measure → split → replace → minify + Brotli → budget).
html: • When scripts run (plain/async/defer/module) · preconnect vs preload vs prefetch · why tree shaking keeps code (CJS, side effects, barrels, dynamic access) · cutting a 1.5 MB bundle (measure → split → replace → minify + Brotli → budget).
deep_html:
Key points

  • Revision episode: four interview questions on loading and bundles.
  • Know when each kind of script runs, the difference between resource hints, why tree shaking sometimes fails, and a plan for cutting a huge bundle.

Interview answer

For loading, I keep the critical path short: inline critical CSS, defer scripts, preconnect to key origins and preload late-discovered critical files. For bundles, I measure first, split by route and feature, replace heavy dependencies, make sure tree shaking works with ES modules, ship minified and Brotli-compressed code, and protect it with a size budget in CI.

Quick quiz

When does each script type run: plain, async, defer, module?

Plain: blocks parsing, runs immediately. async: downloads in parallel, runs on arrival, no order. defer: downloads in parallel, runs after parsing in order. module: deferred by default.

preconnect vs preload vs prefetch?

preconnect warms up a connection to an origin. preload fetches a resource needed by this page at high priority. prefetch fetches a resource for a future navigation at low priority.

Why might tree shaking keep code you don't use?

CommonJS modules, side effects (or missing "sideEffects" config), barrel files that re-export everything, or dynamic access to a namespace import.

How would you cut a 1.5 MB bundle?

Measure with a bundle analyzer → split by route and lazy-load heavy features → replace or remove heavy dependencies and polyfills, dedupe versions → make sure tree shaking works → minify + Brotli → add a size budget in CI so it doesn't grow back.

title: Responsive images
text: srcset (files + w widths) + sizes (display width) → browser picks the smallest sharp file, including DPR. for AVIF/WebP + JPEG fallback and art direction ( media ). See it: Elements → hover : rendered vs intrinsic size; Lighthouse "Properly size images". Trap: no sizes → assumes 100vw → biggest file.
html:
• srcset (files + w widths) + sizes (display width) → browser picks the smallest sharp file, including DPR. <picture> for AVIF/WebP + JPEG fallback and art direction (media).
  • See it: Elements → hover <img>: rendered vs intrinsic size; Lighthouse "Properly size images". Trap: no sizes → assumes 100vw → biggest file.
deep_html:
Key points

  • srcset lists image files with their widths; sizes tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed. The browser picks the smallest file that still looks sharp, including screen density (DPR).
  • <picture> lets you offer modern formats (AVIF/WebP) with a JPEG fallback, or different crops per screen (art direction).
  • Without sizes, the browser assumes the image is full screen width (100vw) and often downloads the biggest file.

Interview answer

For responsive images I provide multiple widths in srcset and describe the rendered width with sizes, so the browser can choose the smallest file that's sharp for the device's pixel density. I use the picture element to serve AVIF or WebP with a JPEG fallback, and for art direction when mobile needs a different crop. I always set width and height to avoid layout shift, and I serve images from an image CDN that resizes and converts automatically.

The analogy

Ordering a pizza by table size. srcset is the menu of sizes; sizes tells the waiter how big your table is. Without that, they bring the family size to a table for one.

How it works

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="/p-400.avif 400w, /p-800.avif 800w, /p-1600.avif 1600w"
          sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw">
  <img src="/p-800.jpg"
       srcset="/p-400.jpg 400w, /p-800.jpg 800w, /p-1600.jpg 1600w"
       sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"
       width="800" height="600" alt="Blue running shoes">
</picture>

Common traps

  • Missing sizes → the browser assumes 100vw and downloads the largest candidate.
  • Using x descriptors for fluid images. 1x/2x suits fixed-size images like logos; use w for layout-dependent ones.
  • Forgetting width/height causes layout shift.

See it yourself

DevTools → Elements → hover an <img>: it shows rendered size vs intrinsic size. If intrinsic is much bigger, you're over-downloading. Lighthouse flags this as "Properly size images".

Quick quiz

What does sizes tell the browser?

How wide the image will be displayed at different viewport widths, so it can choose the right srcset file before layout.

Why use picture instead of just img?

To offer modern formats with fallbacks (AVIF/WebP → JPEG) or different crops for different screens.

A phone (DPR 3) shows an image 360 px wide. Which width should it download?

About 1080 px (360 × 3), so the closest srcset candidate at or above that.

title: LCP image priority
text: Images start Low and are boosted only after layout. fetchpriority="high" on the hero (Chrome team test on Google Flights: LCP 2.6 s → 1.9 s). Must be discoverable by the preload scanner: plain in HTML, or . Never lazy, don't wait for client JS. Trap: high priority on everything = nothing is high priority.
html:
• Images start Low and are boosted only after layout. fetchpriority="high" on the hero (Chrome team test on Google Flights: LCP 2.6 s → 1.9 s).
  • Must be discoverable by the preload scanner: plain <img> in HTML, or <link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high">. Never lazy, don't wait for client JS.
  • Trap: high priority on everything = nothing is high priority.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Images start at Low priority and are only boosted after layout shows they're in the viewport. That's too late for the hero.
  • Add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP image. Google's test on Google Flights improved LCP from 2.6 s to 1.9 s.
  • The image must be discoverable early: a plain <img> in the HTML, or a <link rel="preload">. Never lazy, never waiting on client JS.

Interview answer

Browsers fetch images at low priority until layout confirms they're visible, so the LCP hero often starts downloading late. I put the hero as a real img tag in the server HTML so the preload scanner finds it immediately, add fetchpriority high, and never lazy-load it. If the image is referenced only from CSS or created by JavaScript, I add a preload link with fetchpriority high. I use high priority only for one or two critical images, since marking everything high defeats the purpose.

The analogy

Airport boarding. Normally everyone boards by row, but you can hand the hero image a priority pass so it skips the queue. Give priority passes to everyone and it's just a queue again.

How it works

<img src="/hero-1200.avif" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high" alt="Sale banner">

<!-- Hero only referenced in CSS? Preload it -->
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero-1200.avif" fetchpriority="high">

Common traps

  • fetchpriority="high" on many images = nothing is high anymore.
  • Carousels where the first slide is set by JS: the browser can't find it early.
  • Lazy-loading everything by default, including above-the-fold images.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → enable the Priority column → reload. The hero should show High and start near the top of the waterfall.

Quick quiz

What priority do images normally start with?

Low, boosted to high only once layout shows they're in the viewport.

Why can't the preload scanner find a CSS background hero?

The URL is inside a stylesheet that must be downloaded and parsed first, then matched to elements.

How many images should get fetchpriority="high"?

Usually just the LCP image (one, maybe two).

title: Web fonts
text: FOIT (invisible text while loading) vs FOUT (fallback, then swap). font-display : block · swap · optional. Swap can cause CLS → matched fallback with size-adjust , ascent-override . Arrive sooner: self-host, preload 1–2 files, woff2, subset. IQ: safest for CWV is often optional (no invisible text, no late shift) — trade-off: slow first visits may never show the brand font.
html:
• FOIT (invisible text while loading) vs FOUT (fallback, then swap). font-display: block · swap · optional.
  • Swap can cause CLS → matched fallback with size-adjust, ascent-override. Arrive sooner: self-host, preload 1–2 files, woff2, subset.
  • IQ: safest for CWV is often optional (no invisible text, no late shift) — trade-off: slow first visits may never show the brand font.
deep_html:
Key points

  • While a web font loads, the browser either hides text (FOIT, flash of invisible text) or shows a fallback then swaps (FOUT, flash of unstyled text).
  • font-display controls this: block (hide briefly), swap (fallback now, swap later), optional (use the font only if it's already fast).
  • swap can cause layout shift; fix with a size-matched fallback (size-adjust, ascent-override).

Interview answer

Web fonts can cause invisible text or a visible swap. font-display swap shows a fallback immediately and replaces it, which avoids invisible text but can shift layout if the fonts have different metrics, so I define a fallback font-face with size-adjust and metric overrides to match. To make fonts arrive sooner I self-host woff2 files, subset them, and preload the one or two most important ones. For the best Core Web Vitals, font-display optional avoids both invisible text and late shifts, at the cost of sometimes not showing the brand font on slow first visits.

The analogy

A guest speaker running late. block: the stage stays silent until they arrive. swap: a stand-in starts talking, then the real speaker takes over mid-sentence. optional: if they're not here in time, the stand-in does the whole talk.

How it works

@font-face {
  font-family: 'Inter';
  src: url('/fonts/inter-latin.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-display: swap;
}
@font-face {                        /* fallback sized like Inter, so the swap doesn't shift text */
  font-family: 'Inter Fallback';
  src: local('Arial');
  size-adjust: 107%;
  ascent-override: 90%;
}
body { font-family: 'Inter', 'Inter Fallback', sans-serif; }

Common traps

  • Preloading many fonts competes with the hero image. Preload one or two at most.
  • Google Fonts from another origin adds connection time; self-hosting avoids it.
  • Shipping all character sets. Subset to the scripts you need (e.g. Latin, Devanagari).

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → filter Font → throttle to Slow 4G and reload: watch the text flash or swap. Rendering tab → Layout Shift Regions shows swap shifts.

Quick quiz

FOIT vs FOUT?

FOIT: text is invisible until the font loads. FOUT: fallback text shows first, then swaps to the web font.

How do you prevent layout shift from a font swap?

Use a fallback font-face with size-adjust and ascent/descent overrides so it takes the same space as the web font.

Why can font-display: optional be best for Core Web Vitals?

It never hides text and never swaps late, so no FOIT and no font-related layout shift.

title: Third-party cost
text: Third-party JS runs on your main thread: long tasks (INP), late banners (CLS), extra origins (connections). Measure: DevTools request blocking → compare. Tame: facades, delay until interaction, self-host, Partytown (web worker). See it: Performance "3rd parties" insight. Trap: async only avoids parser blocking; the script still runs on the main thread.
html:
• Third-party JS runs on your main thread: long tasks (INP), late banners (CLS), extra origins (connections).
  • Measure: DevTools request blocking → compare. Tame: facades, delay until interaction, self-host, Partytown (web worker). See it: Performance "3rd parties" insight.
  • Trap: async only avoids parser blocking; the script still runs on the main thread.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Third-party scripts (chat widgets, analytics, ads, A/B tools) run on your main thread: they cause long tasks (INP), late banners (CLS) and extra connections.
  • Measure first: block them in DevTools and compare.
  • Tame them: facades (fake button until clicked), load after interaction, self-host, or move them off the main thread (Partytown).

Interview answer

Third-party scripts compete with my own code for the main thread and the network, so they often cause the worst long tasks and layout shifts. I measure their impact by blocking them and comparing metrics, then decide per script: remove it, load it after the page is interactive or on first interaction, replace heavy embeds with a lightweight facade, reserve space for anything that renders, and in some cases run them in a web worker with a tool like Partytown. Async loading alone doesn't help, because the script still executes on the main thread.

The analogy

Letting a guest cook in your kitchen during dinner rush. Even if they arrive quietly (async), once they start cooking they use your one stove.

How it works

// Load the chat widget only when the user shows intent
chatButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const s = document.createElement('script');
  s.src = 'https://chat.example.com/widget.js';
  document.body.append(s);
}, { once: true });

Common traps

  • "It's async, so it's fine." async only avoids blocking HTML parsing; it still runs on your main thread.
  • Tag managers quietly grow to dozens of scripts. Audit them regularly.
  • Embeds without reserved space (YouTube, chat bubbles, cookie bars) cause CLS.

See it yourself

DevTools → Network → right-click a third-party request → Block request domain → reload and compare the Performance trace. The Performance panel also has a "3rd parties" insight listing their cost.

Quick quiz

Why doesn't async solve third-party performance?

It only prevents parser blocking; when the script runs, it still occupies the main thread.

What's a facade?

A lightweight static placeholder that looks like the widget and loads the real one only when the user interacts with it.

How do you measure one script's impact?

Block its domain in DevTools (or remove it in a test) and compare metrics with and without it.

title: IQ: images, fonts, third parties
text: Why sizes · slow hero LCP checklist (HTML, fetchpriority/preload, not lazy, right size/format/CDN) · no FOIT + no font CLS · adding a chat widget safely (measure, facade, after interaction, reserve space).
html: • Why sizes · slow hero LCP checklist (HTML, fetchpriority/preload, not lazy, right size/format/CDN) · no FOIT + no font CLS · adding a chat widget safely (measure, facade, after interaction, reserve space).
deep_html:
Key points

  • Revision episode: interview questions on images, fonts and third-party scripts.
  • Know why sizes matters, the slow-hero checklist, how to avoid both invisible text and font shifts, and how to add a chat widget safely.

Interview answer

For images I serve responsive, modern formats with srcset and sizes, make the hero discoverable with high priority and never lazy-load it. For fonts I self-host, subset and preload the critical one, with a metric-matched fallback. For third parties I measure their cost and load them late or behind facades, reserving space for anything they render.

Quick quiz

Why does sizes matter on a responsive image?

Without it, the browser assumes the image is 100vw wide and picks a much larger file than needed.

Checklist for a slow hero image (LCP)?

It's an <img> in the HTML (not CSS/JS), has fetchpriority="high" or a preload, isn't lazy-loaded, is correctly sized via srcset/sizes, uses AVIF/WebP, and is served from a CDN.

How do you avoid both invisible text and font layout shift?

Use font-display swap with a size-adjusted fallback font (or optional), self-host and preload the key woff2 file, and subset it.

Marketing wants a chat widget. How do you add it without hurting performance?

Measure its cost, load it behind a facade or after first interaction/idle, reserve space for its button to avoid CLS, and keep it off the critical path. Re-check field INP and CLS after launch.

title: Debounce
text: Run once after the user stops (e.g. 300 ms of quiet). Search boxes, autosave, resize. clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait); Trap: debounce doesn't fix race conditions → AbortController or ignore stale responses.
html:
• Run once after the user stops (e.g. 300 ms of quiet). Search boxes, autosave, resize.
  • clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  • Trap: debounce doesn't fix race conditions → AbortController or ignore stale responses.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Debounce = run the function once, after the user stops for a set time (e.g. 300 ms of quiet).
  • Use it for search-as-you-type, autosave, and window resize recalculations.
  • It reduces calls, but it doesn't fix race conditions: an older response can still arrive after a newer one.

Interview answer

Debouncing delays a function until a burst of events has stopped for a given wait time. Each new event clears the pending timer and starts a new one, so the function runs only once after the last event. It's ideal for search inputs, autosave and resize handling. It reduces work and requests, but responses can still arrive out of order, so I also cancel stale requests with AbortController or ignore responses that don't match the latest query.

The analogy

A lift door. Every time someone else walks in, the door timer restarts. The door closes only after nobody has entered for a few seconds.

How it works

function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  };
}

let controller;
const search = debounce(async q => {
  controller?.abort();                         // cancel the previous request
  controller = new AbortController();
  const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, { signal: controller.signal });
  render(await res.json());
}, 300);

input.addEventListener('input', e => search(e.target.value));

Common traps

  • Race conditions remain. Abort old requests or check the query when the response arrives.
  • Creating a new debounced function on every React render resets it each time. Create it once (useMemo/useRef).
  • Debouncing visual feedback. Debounce the expensive work, not the UI that should respond instantly.

See it yourself

Type in a search box with DevTools → Network open: without debounce you see a request per keystroke; with it, one request after you pause.

Quick quiz

When does a debounced function run?

After no new calls have happened for the wait period, once, with the latest arguments.

Why use AbortController with debounced search?

To cancel older in-flight requests so a slow, stale response can't overwrite newer results.

Debounce vs throttle in one line?

Debounce runs once after activity stops; throttle runs at most once per interval while activity continues.

title: Throttle
text: At most once per interval, steadily during the storm (scroll progress, drag). Debounce = after silence; throttle = regular. Better for visuals: requestAnimationFrame ; for visibility: IntersectionObserver . Trap: naive throttle drops the last call → add a trailing call.
html:
• At most once per interval, steadily during the storm (scroll progress, drag). Debounce = after silence; throttle = regular.
  • Better for visuals: requestAnimationFrame; for visibility: IntersectionObserver.
  • Trap: naive throttle drops the last call → add a trailing call.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Throttle = run at most once per interval, steadily, while the events keep coming.
  • Use it for scroll progress bars, drag handlers, and continuous position updates.
  • Debounce waits for silence; throttle keeps a steady rhythm. For visuals, requestAnimationFrame is often even better.

Interview answer

Throttling limits a function to at most once per time window while events keep firing, which suits continuous interactions like scrolling or dragging where you want regular updates rather than a single update at the end. A naive throttle drops the final event, so I add a trailing call to capture the last state. For anything visual I prefer requestAnimationFrame, which naturally runs once per frame, and for visibility checks I use IntersectionObserver instead of scroll listeners.

The analogy

A metro that leaves every 3 minutes no matter how many people rush in. Debounce would be a metro that only leaves once nobody has entered for 3 minutes.

How it works

function throttle(fn, interval = 100) {
  let last = 0, timer;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now(), remaining = interval - (now - last);
    clearTimeout(timer);
    if (remaining <= 0) { last = now; fn(...args); }
    else timer = setTimeout(() => { last = Date.now(); fn(...args); }, remaining);   // trailing call
  };
}

window.addEventListener('scroll', throttle(updateProgressBar, 100), { passive: true });

Common traps

  • Naive throttle drops the last event, so the final scroll position is never shown. Add a trailing call.
  • Throttling with timers for animation. Use requestAnimationFrame so updates align with frames.
  • Scroll listeners to detect visibility. IntersectionObserver does it without running code on every scroll.

See it yourself

Log inside a scroll handler with and without throttle and scroll quickly: hundreds of logs vs a steady handful.

Quick quiz

Which would you use for a scroll progress bar, debounce or throttle?

Throttle (or requestAnimationFrame), because it needs regular updates while scrolling.

What's the "trailing call" in throttle?

One final call after the last event, so the last state isn't lost when it fell inside the wait window.

What's better than throttling scroll to detect when an element appears?

IntersectionObserver.

title: Virtualization
text: Render only visible rows + overscan; a tall spacer keeps the scrollbar right; rows are recycled. Libraries: TanStack Virtual, react-window. Lighter option: content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size (stays in DOM). See it: Performance monitor → DOM Nodes stays flat. Trap: Ctrl+F misses unrendered rows, screen readers, unknown heights → jumpy scrollbar.
html:
• Render only visible rows + overscan; a tall spacer keeps the scrollbar right; rows are recycled. Libraries: TanStack Virtual, react-window.
  • Lighter option: content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size (stays in DOM). See it: Performance monitor → DOM Nodes stays flat.
  • Trap: Ctrl+F misses unrendered rows, screen readers, unknown heights → jumpy scrollbar.
deep_html:
Key points

  • Virtualization renders only the rows you can see (plus a few extra), not all 10,000.
  • A tall spacer keeps the scrollbar correct, and rows are recycled as you scroll.
  • Lighter option: CSS content-visibility: auto skips rendering off-screen content while keeping it in the DOM.

Interview answer

For very long lists, rendering every row creates thousands of DOM nodes, which slows initial render, scrolling and memory. Virtualization renders only the rows in the viewport plus an overscan buffer, positions them inside a container sized to the full list so the scrollbar is accurate, and swaps content as the user scrolls. Libraries like TanStack Virtual or react-window handle the math. A simpler alternative is content-visibility auto with contain-intrinsic-size. The trade-offs are browser find-in-page, accessibility and variable row heights.

The analogy

A train window. You only see a few metres of track at a time; the track you can't see doesn't need to be painted in front of you, it just needs to be there when you reach it.

How it works

/* Lighter alternative: let the browser skip off-screen rendering */
.row {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 56px;   /* estimated height so scroll size stays stable */
}

Common traps

  • Ctrl+F can't find rows that aren't rendered (with JS virtualization).
  • Screen readers may not know the full list length; set aria-rowcount / aria-setsize.
  • Unknown row heights make the scrollbar jump; measure dynamically or estimate well.

See it yourself

DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Performance monitor → watch DOM Nodes while scrolling a virtualized list: it stays flat. On a normal list it's huge from the start.

Quick quiz

How does a virtualized list keep the scrollbar size correct?

The scroll container contains a spacer with the full list's total height, and visible rows are positioned within it.

What's overscan?

A few extra rows rendered above and below the viewport, so fast scrolling doesn't show blank space.

Name a downside of virtualization.

Browser find-in-page misses unrendered rows; accessibility needs extra work; variable heights are tricky.

title: Web Workers
text: JS on another thread; no DOM; talk via postMessage / onmessage . Good for parsing, image processing, search indexes, crypto, diffing. See it: Performance panel shows a separate Worker track. Trap: postMessage copies data (structured clone) → transfer ArrayBuffer s: postMessage(buf, [buf]) .
html:
• JS on another thread; no DOM; talk via postMessage / onmessage. Good for parsing, image processing, search indexes, crypto, diffing.
  • See it: Performance panel shows a separate Worker track.
  • Trap: postMessage copies data (structured clone) → transfer ArrayBuffers: postMessage(buf, [buf]).
deep_html:
Key points

  • A Web Worker runs JavaScript on another thread, so heavy work doesn't freeze the page.
  • Workers can't touch the DOM. They talk to the page with postMessage and onmessage.
  • Good for parsing big files, image processing, search indexes, encryption, diffing.

Interview answer

Web Workers run scripts in a background thread with their own event loop. They can't access the DOM, but they can do CPU-heavy work like parsing, compression, image manipulation or building search indexes, and communicate with the main thread through postMessage. Messages are copied using structured cloning, which is expensive for large data, so for big binary data I transfer ownership of ArrayBuffers instead of copying. This keeps the main thread free for input and rendering.

The analogy

Hiring a second chef who works in a back kitchen. They can't serve customers (no DOM), but they can do all the heavy chopping and send the results out through a window.

How it works

// main.js
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./search-worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
worker.postMessage({ type: 'build', items });
input.addEventListener('input', e => worker.postMessage({ type: 'query', q: e.target.value }));
worker.onmessage = e => renderResults(e.data);

// search-worker.js
let index = [];
onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  if (data.type === 'build') index = data.items.map(i => ({ ...i, key: i.name.toLowerCase() }));
  if (data.type === 'query') postMessage(index.filter(i => i.key.includes(data.q.toLowerCase())).slice(0, 50));
};

Common traps

  • Copying huge data. postMessage clones by default; transfer ArrayBuffers: postMessage(buf, [buf]).
  • Trying to update the DOM from a worker. Send results back and let the main thread render.
  • Using a worker for tiny tasks. Message overhead can cost more than the work itself.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance → record while the worker runs: it appears on its own Worker track, separate from the Main track.

Quick quiz

Can a Web Worker read document.querySelector?

No. Workers have no access to the DOM.

How do you send a large ArrayBuffer without copying it?

Pass it in the transfer list: worker.postMessage(buf, [buf]). Ownership moves to the worker.

What kinds of work suit a worker?

CPU-heavy, DOM-free work: parsing, compression, image processing, search indexing, crypto, diffing.

title: Why React re-renders
text: State change · context change · parent re-render (props changing is not the trigger). Render ≠ DOM update (commit applies only real changes). Fix structurally: move state down, pass components as children. See it: React DevTools "Highlight updates" + Profiler "Why did this render?". IQ: same value via Object.is → bail out; a new object with the same contents re-renders.
html:
• State change · context change · parent re-render (props changing is not the trigger). Render ≠ DOM update (commit applies only real changes).
  • Fix structurally: move state down, pass components as children. See it: React DevTools "Highlight updates" + Profiler "Why did this render?".
  • IQ: same value via Object.is → bail out; a new object with the same contents re-renders.
deep_html:
Key points

  • A React component re-renders when: its state changes, a context it uses changes, or its parent re-renders.
  • "Props changed" is not the trigger: by default children re-render whenever the parent does.
  • Render ≠ DOM update. React only commits the real differences to the DOM.

Interview answer

A component re-renders when its own state updates, when a context value it consumes changes, or when its parent re-renders, regardless of whether props changed, unless it's memoized. Rendering just means calling the component function to produce a new element tree; React then diffs it and commits only actual changes to the DOM. To reduce unnecessary renders I fix the structure first: move state down to where it's used, or pass expensive children as props so they aren't re-created, and use memoization only where profiling shows it helps.

The analogy

A teacher who asks the whole class to redo their homework whenever one student changes their answer. Most students hand in the same work again (render), and only the changed answer gets updated on the board (DOM commit).

How it works

// Problem: typing re-renders the expensive chart
function Page() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return (<>
    <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
    <ExpensiveChart />
  </>);
}

// Fix: move the state down into its own component
function SearchBox() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />;
}
function Page() { return (<><SearchBox /><ExpensiveChart /></>); }

Common traps

  • Setting state to an equal value: React bails out using Object.is. But a new object with the same contents is a different value and re-renders.
  • "Re-render means the DOM was rebuilt." No, renders are cheap until they're frequent or the component is heavy.
  • Context with a big object re-renders every consumer on any change.

See it yourself

React DevTools → ⚙ → tick Highlight updates when components render. Then use the Profiler → "Why did this render?" to see the cause for each component.

Quick quiz

What are the three causes of a re-render?

Its own state changes, a consumed context changes, or its parent re-renders.

Does a child re-render if its props didn't change?

Yes, when its parent re-renders, unless the child is wrapped in React.memo.

setCount(5) when count is already 5: re-render?

No. React bails out because Object.is(5, 5) is true.

title: Memo myths
text: React.memo (shallow props), useMemo (value), useCallback (function identity). Memo isn't free: storage + comparison every render. Inline objects/arrow functions break memo → stabilize with useMemo/useCallback. Memoize on evidence (Profiler ranked view). Trap: useMemo is a performance hint, never a correctness guarantee — React may discard the cache.
html:
• React.memo (shallow props), useMemo (value), useCallback (function identity). Memo isn't free: storage + comparison every render.
  • Inline objects/arrow functions break memo → stabilize with useMemo/useCallback. Memoize on evidence (Profiler ranked view).
  • Trap: useMemo is a performance hint, never a correctness guarantee — React may discard the cache.
deep_html:
Key points

  • React.memo skips re-rendering a component if its props are shallowly equal. useMemo caches a computed value. useCallback keeps a function's identity stable.
  • Memoization isn't free: it stores values and compares props on every render.
  • Inline objects and arrow functions break memo, because they're new on every render.

Interview answer

React.memo prevents a component from re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal, useMemo caches the result of an expensive calculation between renders, and useCallback caches a function so its reference stays stable. They help only when the skipped work is expensive and the props really are stable, which usually means passing memoized objects and callbacks. Memoization adds memory and comparison overhead, so I apply it based on profiler evidence, not by default. useMemo is a performance hint, not a guarantee.

The analogy

Keeping a photocopy of an answer sheet. Useful if the calculation is long and you check it often. Pointless if the answer takes two seconds to work out, and you still pay for the paper.

How it works

const Row = React.memo(function Row({ item, onSelect }) {
  return <li onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>{item.name}</li>;
});

function List({ items }) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null);
  const onSelect = useCallback(id => setSelected(id), []);
  const sorted = useMemo(() => [...items].sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)), [items]);
  return <ul>{sorted.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} onSelect={onSelect} />)}</ul>;
}

Common traps

  • Memoizing everything adds overhead and makes code harder to read.
  • Relying on useMemo for correctness. React may discard cached values; it's only an optimisation.
  • The React Compiler now does much of this automatically (next episode).

See it yourself

React DevTools → Profiler → record an interaction → Ranked view shows which components took the most time. Memoize those, then record again to compare.

Quick quiz

Why does an inline object prop defeat React.memo?

A new object is created every render, so shallow comparison sees a different reference each time.

useMemo vs useCallback?

useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function reference (useCallback(fn, deps) ≈ useMemo(() => fn, deps)).

When is memoization worth it?

When profiling shows a component or calculation is expensive and it re-renders often with the same inputs.

title: useTransition + React Compiler
text: startTransition(() => setFilter(v)) marks non-urgent updates; renders are interruptible; isPending for subtle feedback. useDeferredValue when you don't own the setter. React Compiler (v1.0, late 2025) auto-memoizes at build time; DevTools shows a "Memo" badge. Trap: transitions don't make work faster, only interruptible → still virtualize / do less.
html:
• startTransition(() => setFilter(v)) marks non-urgent updates; renders are interruptible; isPending for subtle feedback. useDeferredValue when you don't own the setter.
  • React Compiler (v1.0, late 2025) auto-memoizes at build time; DevTools shows a "Memo" badge.
  • Trap: transitions don't make work faster, only interruptible → still virtualize / do less.
deep_html:
Key points

  • startTransition marks a state update as non-urgent. React renders it in the background and can interrupt it if the user types again. isPending lets you show subtle feedback.
  • useDeferredValue does the same when you don't control the state setter (e.g. a prop).
  • The React Compiler (v1.0, late 2025) adds memoization automatically at build time.

Interview answer

useTransition lets me split updates into urgent ones, like updating the input value, and non-urgent ones, like filtering a large list. Updates inside startTransition render at lower priority and are interruptible, so typing stays responsive, and isPending indicates background work. useDeferredValue gives a lagging copy of a value for the same purpose. The React Compiler analyses components at build time and inserts memoization automatically, reducing the need for manual useMemo and useCallback. Neither makes the work itself smaller.

The analogy

A waiter who takes your drink order immediately (urgent) but tells the kitchen the dessert order can wait. If you change your dessert, the kitchen just drops the old one and starts the new one.

How it works

function Search({ allItems }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [results, setResults] = useState(allItems);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function onChange(e) {
    setQuery(e.target.value);                         // urgent: input updates instantly
    startTransition(() => {
      setResults(allItems.filter(i => i.name.includes(e.target.value)));   // can be interrupted
    });
  }

  return (<>
    <input value={query} onChange={onChange} />
    <ul style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>{results.map(r => <li key={r.id}>{r.name}</li>)}</ul>
  </>);
}

// When the value comes from props, defer it instead
const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

Common traps

  • Transitions don't make work faster, only interruptible. Still virtualize big lists and do less.
  • Controlled input inside a transition. Keep the input's own state update outside startTransition.
  • Compiler isn't magic. It skips components that break the Rules of React.

See it yourself

Type quickly into a filter over 10,000 items with and without startTransition (CPU 4x slowdown). Without it, typing lags; with it, the input stays smooth. With the compiler on, React DevTools shows a Memo ✨ badge on optimised components.

Quick quiz

What does startTransition change about an update?

It marks it as non-urgent so React renders it at lower priority and can interrupt it for urgent updates like typing.

When would you use useDeferredValue instead?

When you don't own the state setter, e.g. the value comes in as a prop.

What does the React Compiler do?

It automatically memoizes components and values at build time, reducing manual useMemo/useCallback/React.memo.

title: Chunking long tasks
text: Slice by time (~10 ms), not item count; await scheduler.yield() continues near the front of the queue (setTimeout goes to the back). scheduler.postTask(fn, { priority: 'user-blocking' | 'user-visible' | 'background' }) . See it: many small tasks with gaps instead of one red-cornered block. Trap: await Promise.resolve() is a microtask — it does not yield to rendering or input.
html:
• Slice by time (~10 ms), not item count; await scheduler.yield() continues near the front of the queue (setTimeout goes to the back).
  • scheduler.postTask(fn, { priority: 'user-blocking' | 'user-visible' | 'background' }). See it: many small tasks with gaps instead of one red-cornered block.
  • Trap: await Promise.resolve() is a microtask — it does not yield to rendering or input.
deep_html:
Key points

  • To stop one long task from freezing the page, break it into chunks and yield to the browser between them.
  • Slice by time (~10 ms), not by a fixed item count.
  • await scheduler.yield() continues near the front of the queue; setTimeout goes to the back. await Promise.resolve() does not yield at all (it's a microtask).

Interview answer

I break long work into time-sliced chunks of roughly 5 to 10 milliseconds and yield back to the browser between them, so input and rendering can happen. scheduler.yield is the best option where supported, because the continuation is prioritised ahead of other queued tasks, while setTimeout puts it at the back of the queue. scheduler.postTask lets me set priorities like user-blocking or background. Awaiting a resolved promise doesn't yield, since microtasks run before the browser renders.

The analogy

Mopping a long corridor while people need to walk through. Mop a few metres, step aside to let people pass, then continue, instead of blocking the whole corridor until it's done.

How it works

async function processAll(items) {
  let deadline = performance.now() + 10;
  for (const item of items) {
    process(item);
    if (performance.now() > deadline) {
      await yieldToMain();                      // let input + paint happen
      deadline = performance.now() + 10;
    }
  }
}

function yieldToMain() {
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) return scheduler.yield();
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

// Priorities
scheduler.postTask(() => sendAnalytics(), { priority: 'background' });

Common traps

  • Microtasks don't yield. The browser only renders and handles input between tasks.
  • Fixed item counts. 100 items may take 2 ms on a laptop and 60 ms on a cheap phone; slice by time.
  • Yielding inside a loop that mutates shared state can leave UI half-updated; design chunks to be safe.

See it yourself

DevTools → Performance: one big task with a red corner before; many small tasks with gaps after chunking.

Quick quiz

Why doesn't await Promise.resolve() help a long task?

It schedules a microtask, which runs before the browser can render or process input, so the main thread never gets a break.

Advantage of scheduler.yield over setTimeout?

The continuation goes near the front of the queue, so your work resumes promptly instead of waiting behind other tasks.

Why slice by time instead of by item count?

Device speed varies a lot; a time budget keeps chunks short on slow phones too.

title: Performance budgets
text: Agreed limits, e.g. JS ≤ 170 KB compressed, LCP ≤ 2.5 s, TBT ≤ 200 ms. Kinds: quantity, milestone timings, rule-based scores. Enforce in CI: Lighthouse CI assertions, size-limit → fail the PR. IQ: start from current field data, set slightly better, ratchet down, test on a real mid-range phone.
html:
• Agreed limits, e.g. JS ≤ 170 KB compressed, LCP ≤ 2.5 s, TBT ≤ 200 ms. Kinds: quantity, milestone timings, rule-based scores.
  • Enforce in CI: Lighthouse CI assertions, size-limit → fail the PR.
  • IQ: start from current field data, set slightly better, ratchet down, test on a real mid-range phone.
deep_html:
Key points

  • A performance budget is an agreed limit your team won't exceed, e.g. JS ≤ 170 KB compressed, LCP ≤ 2.5 s, TBT ≤ 200 ms.
  • Types: quantity (KB, number of requests), timings (LCP, INP), rule-based (Lighthouse score).
  • Enforce it in CI so a pull request that breaks the budget fails, just like a failing test.

Interview answer

A performance budget sets limits on things like bundle size, request counts, or metric timings, so performance doesn't slowly regress. I set initial budgets from current field data, slightly better than today, and tighten them over time. They're enforced automatically in CI with tools like Lighthouse CI assertions or size-limit, so a pull request that exceeds the budget fails and the team has to discuss the trade-off before merging.

The analogy

A monthly spending budget. Without one, small purchases add up and you only notice at the end of the month. A budget makes every new expense a conscious decision.

How it works

// .size-limit.json
[{ "path": "dist/assets/index-*.js", "limit": "170 KB" }]

// lighthouserc.json (assertions)
{ "ci": { "assert": { "assertions": {
  "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }],
  "total-blocking-time": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 200 }]
} } } }

Common traps

  • Budgets nobody enforces are just wishes. Put them in CI.
  • Unrealistic budgets get ignored. Start from where you are.
  • Testing only on fast machines. Validate on a real mid-range Android phone.

See it yourself

Add size-limit to a project and run it in a GitHub Action: open a PR that adds a big library and watch the check fail.

Quick quiz

What are the three kinds of performance budgets?

Quantity-based (KB, requests), milestone timings (LCP, TBT, INP), and rule-based (Lighthouse scores).

How do you choose initial budget values?

From current measurements, set slightly better than today, then tighten over time.

How do you enforce a budget?

Automated checks in CI (Lighthouse CI, size-limit, bundler limits) that fail the build when exceeded.

deep_html:
Key points

  • Revision episode: interview questions on runtime performance.
  • Know debounce vs throttle, how to render a 10,000-row table, why React re-renders, and how to fix a 400 ms click handler.

Interview answer

For runtime performance I reduce how often work runs with debounce, throttle or requestAnimationFrame, render less with virtualization, avoid unnecessary React renders by fixing component structure before memoizing, and keep interactions under 200 ms by giving instant feedback and then chunking, deferring or offloading the heavy work.

Quick quiz

Debounce vs throttle, with examples?

Debounce runs once after events stop (search box, autosave). Throttle runs at most once per interval during events (scroll progress, drag). For visuals use requestAnimationFrame; for visibility use IntersectionObserver.

How would you render a table with 10,000 rows?

Virtualize it (render visible rows + overscan), or use content-visibility: auto, or paginate. Mention the trade-offs: find-in-page, accessibility, variable row heights.

Why does a React component re-render, and how do you reduce it?

State change, context change, or parent re-render. Reduce by moving state down, passing children as props, splitting context, memoizing where profiling shows benefit, or using the React Compiler.

A click handler takes 400 ms. How do you fix INP?

Show feedback immediately, then yield (scheduler.yield) before heavy work; chunk the work; move pure computation to a Web Worker; mark non-urgent React updates as transitions; reduce the work itself (virtualize, cache).

title: Finale: one product page, made fast
text: Measure (CWV, field vs lab) → loading (CDN TTFB, critical CSS, defer, preconnect) → bundle (split, lazy, diet, Brotli) → hero (AVIF srcset, fetchpriority) → shifts (reserve space, font fallback) → third parties (facade, delay) → interactions (feedback first, transition, virtualize, worker, chunking) → budget in CI.

deep_html:
Key points

  • Making one product page fast follows a fixed order: measure → loading → bundle → hero image → layout shifts → third parties → interactions → budget.
  • Each step targets a specific metric: TTFB/LCP, INP or CLS.
  • Finish with a budget in CI so the gains don't disappear.

Interview answer

I start with field data to see which Core Web Vital fails. For loading, I serve HTML from a CDN with caching, inline critical CSS, defer scripts and preconnect to key origins. I shrink the bundle with route splitting, lazy features and lighter dependencies, compressed with Brotli. The hero image is a responsive AVIF with fetchpriority high. I reserve space for images, ads and fonts to keep CLS low, put third-party scripts behind facades or after interaction, and keep interactions responsive with instant feedback, transitions, virtualization and workers. Then I lock it in with performance budgets in CI.

The analogy

Servicing a car in the right order: check the dashboard warnings first (measure), then the engine (loading), then lose the extra weight (bundle), then the tyres and alignment (images and shifts), and finally set a service schedule (budget) so it doesn't slide back.

How it works

Common traps

  • Optimising without measuring. Fix the metric that's actually failing first.
  • One-off clean-ups. Without budgets, performance regresses within months.
  • Ignoring mobile. Test on a mid-range Android phone on 4G.

See it yourself

Run PageSpeed Insights on any big e-commerce product page and map each failed audit to one of the steps above.

Quick quiz

What's the first step in improving a slow page?

Measure with field data to find which metric is failing, then use lab tools to find the cause.

Three fixes that improve LCP?

Faster TTFB (CDN, caching), discoverable high-priority hero image, smaller properly sized modern image formats, less render-blocking CSS/JS.

How do you keep a page fast after optimising it?

Performance budgets enforced in CI and ongoing real-user monitoring.

title: What is state
text: State = data your UI remembers right now that can change while the page is open. Rule: if it changes and the screen must show it, it's state. React's idea: UI = f(state) . Trap: don't store what you can compute. const total = items.reduce(...) , not useState(total) → two sources of truth drift. title: The context trap

title: Selectors
text: Selector picks the slice a component needs; component re-renders only when the result changes ( === after every dispatch). title: React Query

title: Cache invalidation
text: After a mutation: qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['addresses'] }) → marks matching queries stale, refetches active ones. Keys are folders: prefix match ( ['addresses'] hits ['addresses', 7] ); exact: true for one key. Or setQueryData with the server's response (skip a round trip). Too little = screens lie; too much = refetch the world. Other tabs: refetch on window focus; BroadcastChannel ; server push (S6).

title: Normalization

title: REST vs GraphQL vs tRPC

In the wild: GitHub (REST + GraphQL), Shopify Storefront (GraphQL), T3-stack apps (tRPC). Trap: GraphQL is not "faster" — fewer round trips, but careless queries are slow and you lose easy caching. Trap: no business rules (pricing etc.) in the BFF — they get copied per BFF and drift. BFF = shaping only.

title: Cursor pagination
text: "10 items older than this one": response has items + opaque nextCursor ; client sends ?after=<cursor> ; null = end. Server: WHERE created_at < :cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 — with an index, page 1000 ≈ page 1. See it: reddit.com/r/javascript.json → "after": "t3_…" . Trap: ties on the sort key skip rows → sort by (created_at, id) and put both in the cursor. Cost: no jump to page 50.

  • Server: WHERE created_at < :cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 — with an index, page 1000 ≈ page 1.
  • See it: reddit.com/r/javascript.json → "after": "t3_…".
  • Trap: ties on the sort key skip rows → sort by (created_at, id) and put both in the cursor. Cost: no jump to page 50.

title: Infinite scroll vs pages
text: Infinite: great for browsing on phones; footer unreachable, back button loses place, memory grows. Pages: hunting, shareable "page 3" URL, crawlable. Middle: Load more . Build: IntersectionObserver on a sentinel with rootMargin: '600px' ; long lists → virtualization (S3E25). Trap: back button → top of feed. Keep loaded pages + scroll position (query cache or URL) and restore; don't refetch from page 1.

title: IQ: pagination
text: Duplicates on page 2 = offset + inserts → cursor. Missing items with timestamp cursor = ties → (created_at, id) . Jump to page 50 → offset (cap the depth). Infinite scroll without scroll listeners → IntersectionObserver + rootMargin (+ virtualization).

title: Waterfalls
text: Request 2 waits for request 1 → staircase in the Network waterfall; each step costs a round trip (~100–300 ms on mobile). React: parent fetches in an effect → renders child → child fetches = fetch-on-render . Fix: start early (route loader, hoist, prefetch) = fetch-then-render. Trap: true dependency (needs user id) → move the join to the server (one endpoint / BFF) so it happens next to the DB.
html:

  • React: parent fetches in an effect → renders child → child fetches = fetch-on-render. Fix: start early (route loader, hoist, prefetch) = fetch-then-render.
  • Trap: true dependency (needs user id) → move the join to the server (one endpoint / BFF) so it happens next to the DB.

title: Parallel requests
text: Independent requests: start all, then await Promise.all([...]) → total ≈ slowest, not the sum. HTTP/2 multiplexes; HTTP/1.1 ≈ 6 connections per host. Promise.all rejects on the first failure (good results lost). Promise.allSettled → {status, value | reason} for each. Trap: await a(); await b(); await c(); is sequential. Create the promises first, then await them together.

title: Race conditions
text: Responses arrive in network order , not request order → an old, slow response can overwrite a newer one. React fix: let ignore = false; … if (!ignore) setX(d); return () => { ignore = true; } . Trap: debounce doesn't fix races (S3E23) — ignore or cancel stale requests; React Query keys data by query.
html:

  • React fix: let ignore = false; … if (!ignore) setX(d); return () => { ignore = true; }.
  • Trap: debounce doesn't fix races (S3E23) — ignore or cancel stale requests; React Query keys data by query.

title: AbortController
text: const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal }); c.abort(); → really stops the request. In effects: abort in the cleanup; ignore AbortError (a cancel isn't a failure). AbortSignal.timeout(5000) for timeouts. See it: Network shows aborted requests as (canceled) . Trap: abort doesn't undo a POST already on the server → idempotency key + status check.

title: Retries + backoff
text: Exponential backoff: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s… capped. Add jitter (random delay) to avoid the thundering herd. Retry network errors, timeouts/408, 429 (after Retry-After), 5xx like 503. Don't retry 400/401/404. React Query: queries retry 3× with min(1000·2^n, 30000) by default; mutations retry 0×. Trap: retry a POST only with an idempotency key.

title: Deduplication
text: Several components ask for the same thing → share the in-flight promise (Map of key → promise, delete on settle). React Query dedups by query key. Dedup ≠ cache: dedup shares a request in flight; cache keeps the answer afterwards. Trap: double fetch in dev = React StrictMode (mount → unmount → mount). Production fetches once.

title: 429 Too Many Requests
text: Rate limits: N requests per user / IP / key per window. Token bucket: each request spends a token; tokens refill steadily. See it: api.github.com headers x-ratelimit-limit: 60 , x-ratelimit-remaining , x-ratelimit-reset (unauthenticated). On 429: read Retry-After and wait. Be a good client: debounce, dedupe, cache. Trap: per-IP limits block whole offices behind one NAT → limit per user / API key.

title: Skeleton screens
text: Skeletons show layout before data → feels faster; must match the real layout or you get CLS (S3E04). Don't flash: show only if loading takes > ~200 ms. Skeleton on first load ( isPending ); on refetch keep old data ( isFetching → small spinner). See it: YouTube with Slow 4G. Trap: actions (saving) → spinner on the button; skeletons are for content.

title: Partial failure
text: An error thrown during render with no boundary unmounts the whole tree. Wrap each widget in an ErrorBoundary with fallback + retry. Data: Promise.allSettled . Decide what's critical (price → error page) vs optional (recommendations → hide). Trap: boundaries don't catch event-handler or async errors → put the error in state and throw during render, or throwOnError in your data library.
